If you want to build a **research-driven Warehouse Management System (WMS)**, don't approach it as just a CRUD application with products, suppliers, and stock quantities. Build it as a system that makes warehouse operations more accurate, efficient, explainable, and intelligent.

The goal should be to study existing warehouse-management research, identify a genuine limitation, design a better approach, and then prove that your approach improves measurable outcomes.

Since you're studying Computer Science and want to build a serious full-stack project, I'd approach this as a combination of **software engineering + operations research + optimization + applied AI**, rather than adding AI everywhere just for the sake of it.

# **1\. The project I would build**

# **SmartStock: Research-Driven Warehouse Intelligence System**

A warehouse platform that manages inventory in real time, recommends where products should be stored, optimizes picking routes, predicts stock shortages, and explains why it recommends a particular action.

(Full-stack project) (Research-driven) (Optimization-focused) (Measurable results)

The differentiator shouldn't be the number of screens. It should be an intelligent decision engine that outperforms a sensible baseline.

For example, a conventional system might store products in fixed locations and let warehouse workers pick them in arbitrary order. Your system could recommend storage locations based on demand, congestion, available space, and picking distance.

Then you test whether those recommendations actually reduce travel distance and picking time.

## **2\. What recent research tells us**

I found several relevant research papers from 2024–2026. These are useful because they show both what researchers have already tried and where a student project could make a meaningful contribution.

**1\. Machine Learning in Warehouse Management: A Survey (2024)**

Procedia Computer Science · DOI: 10.1016/j.procs.2024.02.096

Reviews machine learning for storage-location assignment, warehouse planning, and order picking. It identifies intelligent warehousing as an area with room for further research.

[Read the paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2024.02.096) ·

**2\. Hybrid Genetic Algorithms for Order Assignment and Batching in Picking System (2024)**

IEEE Access · DOI: 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3357689

Reviews methods for assigning orders and grouping them into batches to reduce picking effort and improve resource utilization.

[Read the paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3357689?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ·

**3\. Real-time Task Planning for Order Picking in Intelligent Logistics Warehousing (2025)**

Scientific Reports · Article 7331

Investigates the relationship between order assignment and path planning, making it relevant to a system that must react to changing warehouse conditions.

[Read the open-access paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-88305-9?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ·

**4\. Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Order Picking (2025)**

Computers & Operations Research · Volume 182

Uses a Markov decision process and deep reinforcement learning to adapt order picking to dynamic conditions. The study reports improvements over comparison methods in its experimental setting.

[Read the paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cor.2025.107112) ·

**5\. AI-Enhanced Digital Twin Systems for Warehouse Logistics Optimization (2026)**

ICT Express · Volume 12, Issue 2

Reviews digital twins, AI, inventory management, path planning, and task allocation. It also highlights research opportunities around sustainability, dynamic conditions, and the economic impact of digitalization.

[Read the open-access paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icte.2026.01.009) ·

A useful additional review is [Order Batching Problems: Taxonomy and Literature Review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2023.02.019), published in the _European Journal of Operational Research_ in 2024. It explains how batching, routing, sequencing, and order assignment interact.

## **3\. How to make your system better than existing approaches**

Here is the important part: **don't claim your system is better merely because it uses AI.** Define a problem, establish a baseline, develop an improvement, and test it.

I would choose a research direction that combines four capabilities.

**A. Intelligent inventory placement**

Decide which storage location is best for each SKU (stock-keeping unit) using demand frequency, product size, handling constraints, and distance from packing.

Baseline: random or fixed placement. Proposed improvement: demand-aware, constraint-aware slotting.

**B. Order batching and picking-route optimization**

Group compatible orders and find short routes through warehouse aisles. Account for capacity, order deadlines, and, in an advanced version, congestion.

Baseline: FIFO order processing and a simple aisle traversal. Proposed improvement: heuristic batching and graph-based route planning.

**C. Inventory forecasting and replenishment**

Estimate future demand and identify which items may run out. Generate reorder recommendations using lead time, safety stock, and demand variability.

Baseline: fixed reorder thresholds. Proposed improvement: forecast-informed replenishment, compared against simple baselines.

**D. A warehouse digital twin**

Maintain a virtual representation of the warehouse layout, inventory, open orders, and picker movements. Simulate a proposed strategy before applying it to the operational system.

Baseline: make decisions directly from static reports. Proposed improvement: simulate, compare, and then recommend changes.

My recommendation is to start with A and B, implement the core warehouse workflows, and then add C and a lightweight D. Deep reinforcement learning can be a later experiment, not a prerequisite.

## **4\. The research gap you could investigate**

The literature already covers machine learning, reinforcement learning, picking optimization, and digital twins. So combining these terms alone is not a novel contribution.

One promising hypothesis to investigate is:

Can a constraint-aware warehouse decision engine that combines demand-based storage placement, order batching, and congestion-aware routing reduce total picking distance and completion time compared with standard warehouse heuristics, while maintaining inventory accuracy and respecting operational constraints?

This is a **proposed research question**, not a proven research gap. You must verify its novelty through a systematic literature search before claiming it.

Your possible contribution could be:

- A unified decision engine rather than three unrelated optimization modules.
- Dynamic recommendations when orders, stock, or aisle availability change.
- Explainable decisions: show why a location, route, or replenishment action was recommended.
- A reproducible simulation benchmark with several warehouse sizes and demand patterns.
- A trade-off analysis involving picking time, distance, congestion, and computational cost.

The last two are especially important. A sophisticated algorithm is not automatically better if it takes too long to compute or only works on one artificial layout.

Dashboard · Inventory · Orders · Picking UI · Analytics

Persistent operational data, inventory movements, audit trail, simulation results

For a student project, a modular monolith is a sensible architecture: one deployable backend with clear internal modules. You do not need microservices, Kubernetes, or a distributed database to demonstrate intelligent warehouse optimization.

If you want to use Angular and SQLite, as in your other full-stack project ideas, that is a reasonable localhost prototype stack. Choose a backend framework you can implement reliably; for example, Node.js with TypeScript works well with Angular. The optimization engine can initially live in the same backend, with Python added later if you need its machine-learning and optimization libraries.

One key design decision: **do not maintain stock by simply overwriting a quantity field.** Use controlled stock movements and database transactions, with the current inventory derived or updated consistently. Reservations and picks must not allow two simultaneous orders to consume the same available stock.

## **6\. Build it in phases**

**Phase 1**

Week 1

**Research and problem definition**

Read the papers above. Build a literature matrix containing the problem, method, dataset, assumptions, metrics, limitations, and possible extension. Define a realistic warehouse layout and operational rules.

**Phase 2**

Weeks 2–3

**Build the reliable WMS core**

Implement products, locations, goods receiving, stock transfers, reservations, order creation, picking, packing, dispatch, role-based access, and audit history. Seed realistic sample data so the app works immediately.

**Phase 3**

Weeks 4–5

**Implement optimization baselines**

Represent warehouse aisles as a graph. Implement a shortest-path algorithm, a simple picking heuristic, and demand-based slotting. Record baseline performance before introducing improvements.

**Phase 4**

Weeks 6–7

**Add the proposed approach**

Implement a better batching and routing strategy. Introduce changing order arrivals and configurable aisle restrictions. Add explanations for each recommendation.

**Phase 5**

Weeks 8–9

**Run experiments**

Compare the baseline with your proposed approach across small, medium, and large synthetic warehouses. Test low, normal, and peak demand, and repeat runs with different random seeds.

**Phase 6**

Weeks 10–12\*\*

**Polish and document**

Complete the analytics dashboard, test edge cases, document the architecture and experiments, and prepare a technical report describing what improved, what did not, and the limitations.

These are approximate full-time-equivalent project phases; the schedule may need to be longer alongside college work.

## **7\. How will you prove it is better?**

Your dashboard should display experimental evidence, not invented success percentages.

| **Metric**                 | **What it measures**                                    |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Total picking distance     | Sum of picker travel distance                           |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |
| Order completion time      | Time from order release to completion                   |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |
| Picking productivity       | Lines or units picked per hour                          |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |
| Order fulfillment rate     | Orders completed within the required deadline           |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |
| Inventory accuracy         | Agreement between recorded and simulated physical stock |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |
| Congestion or waiting time | Time lost because of aisle conflicts                    |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |
| Algorithm runtime          | Time taken to produce a recommendation                  |
| ---                        | ---                                                     |

Use the same test scenarios for each method. Include a simple baseline, an established heuristic, and your proposed approach. If feasible, perform an ablation study: remove one component at a time to see whether it actually contributes to the improvement.

For example, if your method reduces picking distance but increases computation time dramatically, report both results. That kind of honest trade-off analysis makes the work more credible.

## **8\. What you should avoid**

- Don't begin with reinforcement learning before you have a working simulator and a baseline.
- Don't claim research novelty simply because you combined AI, IoT, and a digital twin.
- Don't generate arbitrary stock records without realistic dimensions, capacities, demand, and lead times.
- Don't prioritize dashboard animations over transaction correctness and inventory consistency.
- Don't compare your algorithm only against a deliberately weak baseline.
- Don't describe a synthetic-data demonstration as a validated industrial deployment.

# **Warehouse Optimization Research — Deep Research Report**

## **Building a Better Warehouse Robot Optimization System Through Algorithm Design and Analysis**

Your objective is clear now. We are not simply building a Warehouse Management System (WMS). We are investigating how warehouse operations can be optimized beyond existing approaches, studying research papers and industrial systems, identifying limitations, and implementing an algorithm that we can demonstrate performs better under specific conditions.

Since this is your **Design and Analysis of Algorithms (DAA) course project**, the main contribution should be the algorithm, its complexity analysis, and experimental evidence. The application will demonstrate the algorithm rather than become the entire project.

I've researched additional papers, including work published in 2025 and 2026, and found several particularly relevant directions.

My strongest recommendation is to focus on **intelligent task allocation, multi-robot path planning, congestion reduction, and adaptive replanning**.

# **1\. First, Understand What We Are Actually Optimizing**

Your existing eight papers are concentrated on a particular research field: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) and related warehouse robot coordination problems.

That is a good starting point because it gives us a coherent research direction instead of a collection of unrelated warehouse technologies.

A typical robotic warehouse contains multiple interconnected optimization problems.

| **Problem**              | **What needs to be optimized?**                                | **Example**                                                                |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Task allocation          | Which robot should perform which task?                         | Assign a nearby, available robot to a picking task.                        |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Task scheduling          | Which task should be performed first?                          | Prioritize an order with a close deadline.                                 |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Path planning            | What is the shortest or fastest route?                         | Find a route through warehouse aisles.                                     |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Multi-agent coordination | How should multiple robots move together?                      | Prevent two robots from attempting to enter the same narrow aisle.         |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Congestion management    | How can traffic bottlenecks be reduced?                        | Redirect a robot through a less congested aisle.                           |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Deadlock resolution      | How can robots escape mutually blocking situations?            | Resolve two robots blocking each other in a narrow corridor.               |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Dynamic replanning       | How should plans change when the situation changes?            | Recalculate routes when new orders arrive or an aisle becomes unavailable. |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |
| Fleet optimization       | How can the fleet complete more work with available resources? | Coordinate robot assignments, routes, and workstation availability.        |
| ---                      | ---                                                            | ---                                                                        |

These problems are related.

For instance, the nearest robot may not be the best robot to assign a task to. It might need to pass through a congested aisle, while a slightly more distant robot could complete the delivery sooner.

Likewise, finding the shortest route for every robot independently does not necessarily minimize the completion time of the entire fleet.

Research on lifelong MAPF, integrated task scheduling, and robotic warehouse operations explicitly addresses different parts of this problem.

**Our opportunity is to investigate whether better coordination between these decisions can outperform simpler approaches while keeping computational costs manageable.**

## **What about Amazon, Ocado, and other large warehouse operators?**

We should distinguish between industrial systems and publicly available research.

The complete operational algorithms used by commercial warehouse operators are not necessarily public. We cannot honestly claim to have reproduced Amazon's complete internal optimization system or directly beaten a proprietary algorithm that we cannot access.

However, we can study published industrial work, reproduce established algorithms, and compare our approach against them on common benchmark problems.

One especially valuable source is a recent optimization study conducted in collaboration with Amazon Robotics. It addresses robot-task coordination, item-pod assignment, workstation assignment, fulfillment scheduling, and congestion. The paper also provides supplemental materials through its publication page.

That gives us an industrially relevant reference without pretending to know the company's entire internal implementation.

# **2\. Additional Research Papers We Should Study**

I recommend expanding your literature survey beyond the original eight papers.

Below are **11 additional papers or research directions**, selected because they contribute something different to our investigation.

I've prioritized papers that help us understand algorithm design, practical limitations, industrial optimization, benchmarking, and recent developments.

## **Paper 9 — Robotic Warehousing Operations: A Learn-Then-Optimize Approach to Large-Scale Neighborhood Search**

**Authors:** Cynthia Barnhart, Alexandre Jacquillat, Alexandria Schmid  
**Publication:** INFORMS Journal on Optimization  
**Published online:** November 2024; journal issue Summer 2025  
**DOI:** 10.1287/ijoo.2024.0033

Read the publisher's paper and supplementary materials

### **Why this is particularly important**

This research was conducted in collaboration with Amazon Robotics.

Rather than treating pathfinding as an isolated problem, it considers several connected decisions:

- Assigning customer orders to workstations.
- Assigning items and storage pods.
- Scheduling order fulfillment.
- Coordinating robotic activity to reduce congestion and improve throughput.

Its algorithm uses large-neighborhood search combined with a learn-then-optimize strategy. Machine learning estimates which optimization subproblems are promising, while an optimization procedure searches for better solutions.

### **What we should investigate**

The paper demonstrates that warehouse optimization can benefit from coordinating decisions at a higher level than individual robot movements.

Our investigation should examine the relationship between this higher-level scheduling and lower-level collision-free path planning.

For our project, we could implement a smaller, deterministic version of the same general idea: intelligently select which tasks or robots to reconsider instead of recomputing every decision.

That is a potential extension to investigate, not a claim that the paper fails to address these issues.

**Priority for our project: Very high.**

## **Paper 10 — Collaborative Optimization of Task Scheduling and Multi-Agent Path Planning in Automated Warehouses**

**Authors:** Zhang Honglin and colleagues  
**Journal:** Complex & Intelligent Systems, 2023  
**DOI:** 10.1007/s40747-023-01023-5

Read the full paper

### **What does it do?**

This paper explicitly combines task scheduling with multi-agent path planning.

Its approach incorporates:

- An enhanced HEFT algorithm for task scheduling.
- Priority-based conflict resolution for path planning.
- Traffic rules and turning penalties.
- A combined scheduling and path-planning strategy called TS-MAPF.

The authors evaluate their methods in simulated warehouse scenarios involving different numbers of robots and tasks.

### **An important limitation to investigate**

In its conclusion, the paper identifies online and real-time path scheduling as a direction for further research.

That gives us a concrete investigation opportunity.

We should ask:

How does an integrated scheduling and path-planning algorithm perform when new tasks continuously arrive and previously planned routes become less desirable?

We should not assume that the existing approach is necessarily poor at handling such situations. We need to reproduce its assumptions and design experiments that show where it performs well and where it struggles.

**Priority: Very high.**

## **Paper 11 — A Coordinated Scheduling Approach for Task Assignment and Multi-Agent Path Planning**

**Authors:** Chengyuan Fang and colleagues  
**Journal:** Journal of King Saud University – Computer and Information Sciences, 2024  
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jksuci.2024.101930

[Read the publisher's paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jksuci.2024.101930)

### **What does it contribute?**

The authors propose a multilayer planning approach.

The system uses:

1. A genetic algorithm for task allocation.
2. Improved Car-Like Conflict-Based Search for conflict resolution.
3. Spatiotemporal Hybrid-State A\* for path planning.

The design considers multiple tasks and robot motion constraints rather than simply assigning one task and calculating a shortest route. The authors report improved task-completion efficiency and lower computational runtime than their selected baseline.

### **What we should investigate**

The key question is whether the cost of repeatedly coordinating task allocation and conflict resolution becomes significant as workload and congestion increase.

We should investigate the trade-off between solution quality and runtime, especially when the system must make decisions quickly.

For our project, this is also an opportunity to compare a genetic-algorithm-based assignment method with simpler, more computationally efficient heuristics.

**Priority: High.**

## **Paper 12 — Lifelong MAPF for Shipment Preparation in Stochastic Warehouses**

**Authors:** Abderraouf Maoudj, Samir Nadir Mekid, Anders Lyhne Christensen  
**Conference:** IEEE CASE 2024  
**DOI:** 10.1109/CASE59546.2024.10711327

Read the paper's publication record

### **Why should we study it?**

This paper considers an important characteristic of practical warehouses: uncertainty.

Robots may need to complete multiple pickup and delivery tasks before a shipment is ready. Pickup and delivery durations are stochastic rather than perfectly predictable.

The authors introduce a benchmark dataset and a zone-based task assignment algorithm designed to reduce congestion. Their approach combines task allocation with decentralized multi-agent path planning.

### **Our research question**

What happens when task assignment is optimized using estimated travel costs, but the actual execution times differ from expectations?

We could investigate whether a task allocator that incorporates congestion estimates and periodically revises assignments outperforms a static assignment strategy under uncertain task durations.

This is an important direction because a method that works well under deterministic assumptions may behave differently when tasks and delays vary.

**Priority: Very high.**

## **Paper 13 — MAPF-LNS2: Fast Repairing for Multi-Agent Path Finding via Large Neighborhood Search**

**Authors:** Jiaoyang Li and colleagues  
**Conference:** AAAI 2022  
**DOI:** 10.1609/aaai.v36i9.21266

Read the AAAI paper

### **Understand this paper carefully**

MAPF-LNS2 is particularly relevant if we want to develop an improved algorithm rather than merely combine existing shortest-path algorithms.

Its basic idea is to begin with paths that contain conflicts and repeatedly select a subset of agents whose paths need to be repaired.

It replans those agents to reduce conflicts while preserving as much of the existing solution as possible.

The authors report that MAPF-LNS2 can achieve near-optimal solutions on many benchmark instances while solving difficult instances more quickly than the competing methods they evaluated.

### **The potential opportunity**

Instead of recalculating every robot's route whenever the warehouse becomes congested, can we intelligently identify and replan only the most problematic subset of robots?

We could investigate:

- Which robots should enter the replanning neighborhood?
- Should we choose agents with repeated conflicts or agents blocking high-traffic aisles?
- How large should the replanning neighborhood be?
- How does the choice affect runtime and total completion time?

This gives us a concrete algorithm-design problem that fits a DAA course very well.

**Priority: Essential.**

## **Paper 14 — Which MAPF Model Works Best for Automated Warehousing?**

**Authors:** Sumanth Varambally, Jiaoyang Li, Sven Koenig  
**Conference:** Symposium on Combinatorial Search, 2022  
**DOI:** 10.1609/socs.v15i1.21767

Read the paper

### **Why it matters**

Traditional MAPF methods often simplify robot movement. For example, they may assume that a robot can move from one grid cell to an adjacent cell in a single time step.

Real robots have more complex dynamics. Turning, timing errors, and imperfect execution can affect their ability to follow planned paths.

This paper examines multiple MAPF formulations, including models that account for rotation, robustness, and continuous time. The authors evaluate their effectiveness in realistic warehouse simulations using Gazebo.

### **What we should investigate**

We should not evaluate our algorithm only on a grid where every movement has identical cost.

A more realistic simulator should allow us to experiment with:

- Different travel times.
- Turning penalties.
- Narrow corridors.
- Delayed movements.
- Conflicting reservations.

We can start with a grid-based implementation and add realistic movement costs gradually.

This makes the project more convincing without requiring physical robots.

**Priority: High.**

## **Paper 15 — Optimal and Bounded-Suboptimal Multi-Goal Task Assignment and Path Finding**

**Authors:** Xinyi Zhong, Jiaoyang Li, Sven Koenig, Hang Ma  
**Conference:** IEEE ICRA 2022  
**DOI:** 10.1109/ICRA46639.2022.9812020

Read the publication record

### **Why we need it**

This paper studies the problem of assigning sequences of goals to multiple agents while simultaneously determining collision-free paths.

The authors formally establish that optimal multi-goal task assignment and pathfinding is NP-hard, and present optimal and bounded-suboptimal algorithms.

This is important for our DAA report.

We should understand the distinction between:

- An algorithm that guarantees an optimal solution but may take too long.
- An algorithm that quickly finds a good solution but does not guarantee global optimality.
- An algorithm that finds collision-free solutions but may produce inefficient routes.

These are different properties.

**Priority: High for theoretical analysis.**

## **Paper 16 — An Empirical Evaluation of Learning-Based Multi-Agent Path Finding Algorithms in Warehouse Environments**

**Authors:** Andrea Giuffrida, Nicola Basilico, Francesco Amigoni  
**Journal:** Robotics and Autonomous Systems, 2025  
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.robot.2025.105149

Read the paper

### **What makes it valuable?**

This study compares learning-based MAPF algorithms against traditional search and planning techniques in warehouse-like environments.

The authors report that some learned methods approach the performance of conventional algorithms in path quality while requiring relatively little computation during execution. However, their analysis also identifies issues that require further work, including nonzero collision rates in learning-based approaches and evaluation in dynamically changing environments. Physical robot deployment is another future direction.

### **What we should investigate**

This creates an opportunity to compare computational efficiency against reliability.

A learned algorithm might select routes quickly, but our evaluation should also examine whether those routes remain safe and valid when agents interact in a narrow warehouse layout.

For our DAA project, this paper is particularly useful as a reason to examine hybrid approaches that retain deterministic collision checking while improving decision-making efficiency.

**Priority: Very high.**

## **Paper 17 — Learning-Guided Prioritized Planning for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding in Warehouse Automation**

**Authors:** Han Zheng, Yining Ma, Brandon Araki, Jingkai Chen, Cathy Wu  
**Journal:** Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 2026  
**DOI:** 10.1613/jair.1.20611

[Read the journal paper](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.20611?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

### **What is the new idea?**

The paper introduces RL-RH-PP, which combines reinforcement learning with rolling-horizon prioritized planning.

Instead of always assigning robot priorities using a fixed rule, a learned policy dynamically determines priority orderings.

The authors report the highest total throughput among the baselines they evaluate, with improvements in handling congestion and generalization across different warehouse layouts.

### **How can this help our project?**

It shows that the order in which robots plan their routes can itself be an optimization variable.

We could investigate a simpler alternative that does not require training a neural network:

**Dynamically calculate robot priorities from urgency, waiting time, congestion, and expected delay.**

This would give us an interpretable algorithm that is easier to implement in C++ and analyse theoretically.

We would need to test whether this heuristic can capture some of the benefits of learned prioritization.

We should not assume it will outperform the learned approach without experiments.

**Priority: Very high.**

## **Paper 18 — From Gridworlds to Warehouses: Adapting Lightweight One-Shot Multi-Agent Pathfinding for AGVs**

**Authors:** Hiroki Nagai, Keisuke Okumura  
**Conference:** IJCAI 2026  
**DOI:** 10.24963/ijcai.2026/35

Read the IJCAI paper

This is one of the most recent papers I found that directly addresses the relationship between algorithmic MAPF models and real warehouse robot behaviour.

### **What does it investigate?**

The paper introduces a formulation called multi-agent warehouse pathfinding, designed to account for more realistic automated guided vehicle (AGV) movement.

Its constraints include straight-line movement, in-place rotations with nonzero time costs, acceleration and deceleration, and follower collisions.

The authors adapt Prioritized Planning, LNS2, PIBT, and LaCAM and compare their performance. Their experiments report a trade-off: Prioritized Planning and LNS2 struggle to scale to many agents under their formulation, while PIBT-based approaches achieve better scalability at the expense of solution cost.

### **Why this is significant**

It directly challenges the idea that an algorithm that performs well on a simplified grid will necessarily perform equally well under realistic movement constraints.

We can use this paper to design experiments that vary robot density and movement costs, rather than reporting results from just one easy scenario.

**Priority: Essential for the latest research section of our literature survey.**

## **Paper 19 — Multi-Agent Path Finding Using Conflict-Based Search and Structural-Semantic Topometric Maps**

This is an additional paper that you should keep separate from your original Conflict-Based Search reference.

**Authors:** Scott Fredriksson, Yifan Bai, Akshit Saradagi, George Nikolakopoulos  
**Preprint:** arXiv, 2025  
**Conference:** Accepted for ICRA 2025  
**arXiv:** 2501.17661

[Read the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17661)

It proposes using a sparse topometric map—representing structures such as intersections, pathways, and dead ends—instead of running Conflict-Based Search directly on a large grid map.

It also accommodates continuous-time movement and evaluates the approach in simulation and real multi-robot experiments. The authors report improvements in computational efficiency over traditional CBS in their evaluated scenarios.

### **Our potential takeaway**

The map representation itself may affect optimization performance.

Instead of representing every small space as a separate node, we could investigate whether simplifying the warehouse graph into meaningful intersections, corridors, and storage regions reduces planning overhead.

For an initial DAA project, I would treat this as a later extension because constructing and validating a topometric map introduces additional complexity.

# **4\. What Gaps Can We Identify Across These Papers?**

This is the most important part of the research.

We should not start by declaring that a paper is flawed. We should identify its assumptions, the conditions under which its method is evaluated, and the situations in which those assumptions might limit performance.

The limitations below are **candidate research gaps** supported by the literature we've reviewed. They still need to be checked against the complete papers and their experiments before we claim novelty.

## **Gap A: Task allocation and path planning need to work together**

Some research treats task assignment and path planning as separate problems. Other studies explicitly integrate them.

The 2023 collaborative-optimization paper argues that the decisions are coupled and proposes an integrated solution. The 2024 coordinated-scheduling paper also combines assignment with path planning. The Amazon Robotics collaboration takes integration further into workstation assignments, item-pod assignments, fulfillment scheduling, and congestion management.

Therefore, **simply combining task allocation and path planning is not a sufficiently novel contribution by itself**.

### **The opportunity**

Investigate whether a computationally inexpensive task allocator can incorporate predicted path congestion into its decisions, so that assigning a task to a robot considers not only distance but also the expected effects on the rest of the fleet.

For example:

- Robot A is 10 units away from the pickup location.
- Robot B is 14 units away.
- Robot A would use a heavily congested aisle.
- Robot B has a clear route.

The shortest-distance assignment would choose A. A congestion-aware allocator might choose B if doing so reduces the overall completion time.

We can test this hypothesis directly.

## **Gap B: Scalability versus solution quality**

This is an especially promising direction for a DAA project.

The literature demonstrates that different algorithms trade off solution quality, runtime, and scalability.

For example, the 2026 IJCAI paper reports that Prioritized Planning and LNS2 struggle with increasing agent counts under more realistic movement constraints, while the evaluated PIBT-based approaches offer better scalability at the cost of solution quality.

CBS, meanwhile, is an important reference for collision-free multi-agent planning, but its search can become expensive on difficult instances. MAPF-LNS2 was proposed in part to improve the practical efficiency of planning.

### **The opportunity**

We could design an algorithm that dynamically decides **when to use a cheap planning method and when to spend additional computation resolving difficult conflicts**.

In lightly congested conditions, it could use efficient prioritized planning. When a local group of robots repeatedly conflicts, it could apply a more expensive repair procedure to just that group.

This is a hypothesis we would test against established algorithms.

It is a much stronger research question than simply claiming that our proposed method is faster.

## **Gap C: Dynamic changes and online replanning**

Warehouses do not receive all their work at the beginning of the day.

New tasks may arrive while robots are executing existing routes. Aisles can become unavailable, pickups can take longer than expected, and other robots can block planned movements.

The 2023 collaborative-optimization paper explicitly identifies online and real-time path scheduling as a direction for further research. The 2025 learning-based MAPF evaluation also highlights dynamically changing environments as a direction for future investigation.

Other work already studies lifelong MAPF and stochastic shipment preparation, so we must not describe dynamic replanning as an entirely unaddressed problem.

### **The opportunity**

Evaluate how an algorithm adapts when the environment changes after initial planning.

We can generate scenarios in which:

- Orders arrive continuously.
- Some tasks have tighter deadlines.
- A normally available aisle becomes blocked.
- Pickup or delivery durations vary.
- Several robots encounter the same bottleneck.

Then measure how much the algorithm's performance deteriorates, how quickly it recovers, and how much computation is needed to restore good routes.

## **Gap D: Practical movement constraints**

Simplified grid models do not capture every real robot behaviour.

The 2024 ECAI paper _Multi-Agent Path Finding with Real Robot Dynamics and Interdependent Tasks for Automated Warehouses_ addresses realistic robot trajectories and interdependent pickup and delivery tasks. The 2026 IJCAI paper also adapts MAPF algorithms to more realistic AGV movement constraints.

Consequently, we should not claim that existing MAPF work generally ignores real robot dynamics.

### **The opportunity**

Study the trade-off between model realism and algorithmic efficiency.

We could begin with a graph-based movement model and progressively introduce turning costs, delayed movements, and restrictions on following robots too closely.

The main question would be whether our algorithm remains effective as those constraints increase.

## **Gap E: Performance evaluation is not just about shortest paths**

A route can be short but contribute to poor overall warehouse performance if it causes traffic to accumulate in a busy aisle.

Similarly, a method that maximizes throughput during peak demand might impose excessive waiting on a subset of tasks.

The Amazon Robotics collaboration explicitly considers throughput, workstation workload, and facility congestion, demonstrating the importance of operational metrics beyond path length.

### **The opportunity**

Develop a benchmark that compares the same algorithms across multiple metrics:

| **Metric**                  | **Why we need it**                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Total travel distance       | Measures total movement effort.                                           |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |
| Makespan                    | Measures how long the workload takes to complete.                         |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |
| Throughput                  | Measures how much work is completed per unit of time.                     |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |
| Planning runtime            | Measures whether the algorithm can produce routes quickly enough.         |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |
| Congestion and waiting time | Measures delays caused by conflicts and bottlenecks.                      |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |
| Failed or delayed tasks     | Measures whether the method remains effective during difficult scenarios. |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |
| Maximum task waiting time   | Helps reveal whether some tasks are repeatedly neglected.                 |
| ---                         | ---                                                                       |

This would let us identify algorithms that are genuinely useful, rather than those that optimize just one metric.

# **5\. The Research Direction I Recommend**

After reviewing these studies, I would not try to solve every warehouse optimization problem at once.

I recommend investigating the following question:

**Can an adaptive, congestion-aware, rolling-horizon planning algorithm that selectively repairs local conflicts improve warehouse fleet throughput and task-completion time while maintaining collision-free routes and controlling computation time, compared with established MAPF approaches?**

This is our proposed research question, not a claim that the method is already novel or will outperform existing algorithms.

Before calling it a contribution to research, we must check whether the particular combination has already been studied and determine how our method differs from prior work.

### **Why choose this direction?**

It brings together the most useful themes in our literature:

- Lifelong MAPF and rolling-horizon planning.
- CBS and conflict resolution.
- LNS2 and selective local replanning.
- Congestion-aware assignment and scheduling.
- Research into the trade-off between scalability and route quality.

It also fits a DAA project because it gives us algorithms to implement, compare, analyse, and potentially improve.

## **A possible algorithm to investigate**

We can provisionally call our candidate **Adaptive Congestion-Aware Rolling-Horizon Planning with Local Conflict Repair**, or ACRH-LCR.

This is only a working name for our proposed approach. The final name and contribution should be decided after we review the related algorithms more thoroughly.

The algorithm would have five main stages.

**Stage 1: Assign tasks intelligently**

For each available robot, calculate the cost of serving eligible tasks. Consider travel distance, task urgency, estimated congestion, and relevant robot constraints.

Rather than assigning every task to the nearest robot, select assignments that are expected to produce good overall performance.

**Stage 2: Determine robot priorities dynamically**

Determine which robot should plan first using information such as:

- Time already spent waiting.
- Deadline urgency.
- Whether the robot is likely to block a busy aisle.
- Expected travel and service time.

The priority score should be explicitly defined and tested. We should not assume that a complicated score is automatically better.

**Stage 3: Plan collision-free routes**

Use a shortest-path algorithm such as A\*, extended with time and reservation constraints, to generate routes for each robot.

The reservation mechanism must prevent prohibited vertex conflicts and edge-swap conflicts.

**Stage 4: Repair difficult conflicts selectively**

If a group of robots encounters repeated conflicts or a congested bottleneck, identify the problematic agents and replan their routes.

This would be inspired by large-neighborhood search, but we would need to define our neighborhood-selection and repair rules precisely.

**Stage 5: Replan as conditions change**

As new tasks arrive or the warehouse changes, update assignments and routes within a rolling planning horizon.

A safety layer should validate the resulting plans before the simulator executes them.

The intended advantage is that straightforward situations receive inexpensive planning, while difficult situations receive more targeted optimization.

We must test whether the computational savings and operational improvements justify the added algorithmic complexity.

### **Why include CBS if we expect it to be expensive?**

It provides a useful reference on smaller problems. We can compare solution quality and runtime where it completes successfully, then report timeouts or memory limits on larger problems.

An algorithm should not be declared inferior simply because it is computationally expensive, nor should an algorithm be declared superior merely because it returns a quick solution.

Both solution quality and computational cost matter.

# **7\. How Should We Evaluate the Algorithms?**

We need a repeatable experimental procedure.

## **Start with standard warehouse benchmarks**

The Moving AI Lab provides benchmark maps and problem instances for multi-agent pathfinding, including warehouse layouts. Some of the larger warehouse maps have thousands of traversable states and benchmark scenarios involving hundreds or up to 1,000 agents.

These are valuable because we can test against established instances rather than inventing every test case ourselves.

However, standard MAPF benchmarks do not automatically model every warehouse feature. We can supplement them with our own scenarios for continuously arriving tasks, turning delays, and changing aisle availability.

## **Use multiple workloads**

Test low, medium, and high robot densities. For the initial implementation, something like 10, 25, 50, and 100 robots would be a reasonable starting point, subject to the actual implementation's capabilities.

Then increase the workload where computational resources permit.

We should also test:

| **Scenario**               | **What we are investigating**                                             |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Normal operations          | Typical route planning and task execution.                                |
| ---                        | ---                                                                       |
| High congestion            | Whether our algorithm handles bottlenecks effectively.                    |
| ---                        | ---                                                                       |
| Burst of incoming orders   | Whether it adapts when workload increases suddenly.                       |
| ---                        | ---                                                                       |
| Blocked aisle              | Whether it can recover from a disruption.                                 |
| ---                        | ---                                                                       |
| Unequal robot speeds       | Whether its decisions remain effective with heterogeneous movement costs. |
| ---                        | ---                                                                       |
| Variable service durations | Whether uncertain task execution affects performance.                     |
| ---                        | ---                                                                       |

Every algorithm should face the same maps, tasks, and initial conditions.

Where randomness is involved, use the same collection of random seeds for every algorithm.

## **Establish success criteria before running experiments**

For example, we might specify that our proposed algorithm should:

- Maintain valid, collision-free routes under the defined movement model.
- Improve throughput or makespan relative to the strongest baseline on our target scenarios.
- Stay within a defined planning-runtime budget.
- Avoid severe deterioration in task waiting times.
- Remain effective when congestion or demand increases.

We should not choose success criteria after seeing the results just to make our algorithm look better.

Also, if an algorithm never produces a collision-free plan, we must not silently exclude those failures from the comparison.

# **8\. The DAA Analysis Must Be a Major Part of the Project**

Since this is a Design and Analysis of Algorithms course project, the theoretical analysis cannot be an afterthought.

Let:

- VV be the number of spatial nodes in the warehouse graph.
- EE be the number of graph edges.
- nn be the number of robots.
- HH be the planning horizon, measured in discrete time steps.
- kk be the number of robots selected for local replanning.
- RR be the number of local-repair iterations.

If A\* is applied to a time-expanded graph, its effective search space grows with the planning horizon. A rough bound for one search using a binary heap is:

O(H(∣V∣+∣E∣)log⁡(H∣V∣))O\\left(H(|V|+|E|)\\log(H|V|)\\right)

The actual bound depends on graph construction, edge costs, duplicate-state handling, and the time representation.

A simple prioritized planner that plans routes for all nn robots sequentially could have an approximate bound of:

O(nH(∣V∣+∣E∣)log⁡(H∣V∣))O\\left(nH(|V|+|E|)\\log(H|V|)\\right)

If local repair performs RR rounds of replanning, each involving kk agents, a rough additional cost is:

O(RkH(∣V∣+∣E∣)log⁡(H∣V∣))O\\left(RkH(|V|+|E|)\\log(H|V|)\\right)

These are preliminary estimates for a simplified implementation, not a proven bound for our proposed algorithm. We must refine them once its exact search and repair procedures are defined.

CBS also needs separate analysis because its conflict-tree search can have exponential worst-case behaviour.

Our final report should include:

1. The problem formulation.
2. The algorithm's design and pseudocode.
3. The time and space complexity of every important component.
4. The assumptions under which the analysis holds.
5. Experimental results alongside the theoretical discussion.
6. An explanation of where the proposed algorithm performs well and where it does not.

This makes the project about algorithm design rather than just building an application with a sophisticated-looking dashboard.

# **9\. What Our Final Project Should Contain**

I suggest dividing the project into three connected components.

### **Component A: Warehouse simulator**

A warehouse grid or graph, robot positions, shelves, pickup locations, delivery stations, incoming tasks, and movement restrictions.

It should be able to execute an algorithm's planned routes and record what actually happens.

### **Component B: Algorithm engine**

Implement the baseline algorithms first, then our proposed approach.

Keep the warehouse state, task assignment, pathfinding, conflict detection, and route execution logically separate. That will make it easier to compare algorithms under the same conditions.

### **Component C: Evaluation dashboard**

Show the warehouse layout and robot movements, alongside metrics such as throughput, travel distance, makespan, congestion, planning runtime, and task waiting times.

The dashboard should visualize measured results. It should not generate illustrative improvement percentages that have not been demonstrated experimentally.

An Angular frontend with a suitable backend would work well if you want a full-stack showcase. However, the core simulator and algorithm evaluation should be runnable independently of the UI so that we can reproduce experiments reliably.

# **My Recommendation**

The most promising direction for our course project is:

**An adaptive warehouse fleet optimizer that combines congestion-aware task allocation, rolling-horizon path planning, and selective conflict repair.**

The strongest starting papers for this direction are the Amazon Robotics collaboration on learn-then-optimize warehouse operations, MAPF-LNS2, the lifelong MAPF work, the 2024 stochastic-warehouse study, and the recent papers on learning-guided planning and realistic AGV constraints. They collectively provide useful ideas about integrated optimization, scalable search, uncertainty, and practical robot movement.

**Our next task should be to construct the comparative literature matrix for all 19 entries, then narrow it to a defensible research gap before writing the algorithm.** The key is to find a specific improvement we can implement, analyse, and measure—not to combine as many advanced techniques as possible.

**We should develop our own improved algorithm, but we should NOT invent everything from scratch.** We will study existing algorithms, understand their weaknesses, and design an improved version that we can test against them.

That is the right approach for your DAA course project.

There is one important distinction: combining existing algorithms is not automatically a new research contribution. We need to identify a specific limitation and design a meaningful improvement. We should verify its novelty against the literature before claiming that our algorithm is new.

Let's organize everything clearly.

# **1\. Which algorithms are we using?**

We have three categories: existing algorithms for comparison, existing algorithms that inspire our approach, and our proposed algorithm.

| ---                             | ---                                                                                           | ---                                                          |

These are established approaches, not algorithms we are claiming to have invented. RHCR was developed for lifelong multi-agent pathfinding, while MAPF-LNS2 uses large-neighborhood search to repair conflicting paths.

## **2\. What exactly will our own algorithm do?**

Let's use a temporary name:

**CA-RHPP: Congestion-Aware Rolling-Horizon Prioritized Planning**

This is a working name, not a confirmed novel algorithm. We will finalize its design and name after examining the literature more thoroughly.

Imagine a warehouse with 50 robots, continuously arriving orders, and several narrow aisles.

A basic planner might assign priorities using a fixed rule and plan routes sequentially. Our proposed approach would investigate whether better priority decisions and selective replanning can improve overall warehouse performance.

The algorithm would have four main ideas.

**1\. Congestion-aware decisions**

Estimate congestion along candidate routes instead of considering travel distance alone.

**2\. Adaptive robot priorities**

Determine which robots should receive priority using factors such as urgency, waiting time, and the expected effect on congestion.

**3\. Rolling-horizon replanning**

Repeatedly update plans as robots execute tasks and new work arrives.

**4\. Selective replanning**

When persistent conflicts occur, investigate whether replanning only the affected robots performs better than recalculating every route.

These are proposed design choices. We must check how closely existing research already implements them before presenting the combination as our contribution.

# **3\. How will our algorithm differ from existing algorithms?**

Consider this example:

There are three robots approaching the same narrow aisle.

A fixed-priority planner may repeatedly give one robot precedence. Another robot may have to wait, causing its delivery to miss a deadline.

Our proposed algorithm could consider:

- How long each robot has already waited.
- Whether its task is urgent.
- The congestion expected along its route.
- Whether changing its route would delay other robots.

It could then revise the planning priorities.

**Our research question is whether these adaptive decisions produce measurable improvements over established planning methods.**

We are not assuming that they will. That is what our experiments must establish.
