Executive Summary

We survey 18–19 key MAPF and warehouse optimization papers (2008–2026) covering both academic algorithms and industrial implementations. These include seminal works on Kiva's warehouse system, RHCR for lifelong MAPF, CBS-based solvers, realistic-dynamics planning, and large-scale optimization (e.g. learn-then-optimize search). Table 1 compares each paper by objectives, model assumptions, and results (columns: Objective, Movement, Task, Coordination, Scale, Industrial). Table 2 (the "literature matrix") further cross-tabulates features: e.g. sum-of-costs vs makespan, grid vs continuous models, single-goal vs lifelong tasks, integrated vs separate task/path coordination, reported robot counts, and discussion of industrial systems.

We find that most MAPF research assumes simplified discrete-grid models and treats task allocation and path planning separately. For example, Wurman et al. (2008) describe coordinating ~500–1500 robots with moveable shelves, but with only high-level discussion of algorithms. Li et al. (2021) introduce Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution (RHCR) for lifelong MAPF, efficiently planning for up to ~1000 agents. Sharon et al. (2015) gave the first optimal CBS (Conflict-Based Search) solver, which finds minimum-sum-of-costs paths but assumes discrete moves on grids. Other works add heuristics (e.g. ICBS), decoupled task scheduling (Li et al. – MAPF-LNS2), or learning. Recent contributions address realism and tasks: e.g. Lehoux-Lebacque et al. (ECAI 2024) include continuous dynamics, turning, and heavy loads, using "Interleaved Prioritized Planning" plus a novel Via-Point Star (VP\*) planner. Coop-MAPF (Greshler et al. 2021) adds cooperative tasks (e.g. robot meetings) beyond collision avoidance. Integrated task&path approaches (Zhang et al. 2023; Xu et al. 2026) combine enhanced HEFT scheduling with MAPF, showing good performance on tests.

Across papers, benchmarks vary: grid warehouses, video-game maps, or custom layouts. Robot counts range from ~10s (small labs) to hundreds or thousands (simulations). Common metrics include flowtime (sum-of-costs), makespan, and throughput (orders/min). Key results include: RHCR outperforms prior lifelong MAPF solvers at ~1000 agents; TA-MAPD algorithms reduce makespan vs online baselines; MAPF-LNS2 solves "80% of hardest benchmark instances" in 5 minutes, scaling to ~8000 agents on congestion maps; and the hybrid learn-optimize approach of Barnhart et al. (2024) yields stronger throughput in Amazon-like tasks. However, all note limitations: simplified dynamics (grid/world assumptions), need for fixed task sets, or computation time. Reproducibility varies: some papers provide code (e.g. MAPF-LNS2 on GitHub), while others are conceptual or use proprietary datasets (Kiva).

We also consider industrial implementations. Amazon's early Kiva system is documented by Wurman et al.; later Amazon Robotics studies (e.g. persistent execution frameworks, learn-optimize in collaboration with Amazon) map to academic MAPF models. For example, Varambally et al. (2022) simulate warehouse robots in Gazebo and discuss how the industry-standard reservation/ADG framework relates to MAPF variants. Other industries (e.g. Ocado) use optimization+queues, but public details are scarce. We correlate these with academic methods where possible (e.g. Amazon's use of lifelong planning with robust execution).

Finally, we identify 8 research gaps from the literature: integration of real robot dynamics into MAPF; fully joint task-assignment and path-planning at scale; robust lifelong MAPF under uncertainty/delays; learning-guided planning for large fleets; scalability of integrated algorithms to 1000+ robots; multi-goal and cooperative tasks; and heterogeneous agents (e.g. collaborative dual-robot teams). For each, we propose a specific research question (listed later) and cite supporting papers. We prioritize gaps by projected impact (e.g. real-world applicability) and feasibility for a DAA project.

In summary, this survey synthesizes the problem formulations, algorithms, and benchmarks of modern MAPF/warehouse research, compares academic and industrial approaches, and highlights open questions for improved warehouse management systems.

Literature Survey

Below we summarize each of the 18–19 specified papers in a uniform format: title; authors; year; venue/DOI; problem statement; model (inputs/outputs/constraints); algorithms; assumptions; evaluation (benchmarks, robot counts, metrics); main results; limitations; reproducibility notes. (Where exact details were unavailable, we describe as given in the papers.)

Coordinating Hundreds of Cooperative, Autonomous Vehicles in Warehouses (Wurman et al., 2008)

Venue: AI Magazine 29(1) (Kiva Systems / Amazon Robotics); no public code.

Problem: Design of Kiva's warehouse robot system. Robots move pods (storage shelves) between inventory and workstations to fulfill order picks. The key tasks include scheduling which pod to bring next and planning robot motions.

Model: Simplified: warehouse floor as grid; pods stored in a 2D grid, each robot picks up/ drops off pods at grid nodes. Workers pick items at stations. Input: continuous stream of order requests (each a set of SKUs on pods). Output: assignments of robots to pod retrieval tasks and collision-free paths. Constraints: dynamic obstacles (other robots), limited docking stations.

Algorithms: Not a single algorithmic contribution paper; rather an overview of the system. Mentions that many MAPF and task-allocation subproblems arise (e.g. allocating pods to stations, coordinating traffic), but algorithmic details are proprietary. They emphasize the use of simulation ("AlphabetSoup") for development.

Assumptions: Uniform robot kinematics, grid layout, known shelves and order distribution (order requests assumed Poisson/random). All pods considered identical carriers.

Evaluation: Simulations of large-scale warehouses: e.g. up to 150 picking stations, 1500 robots, and 20,000 pods. Real deployment: first customer in 2006 with >150 robots.

Results: Reported "a factor of two or more" improvement in pick-and-pack throughput compared to manual systems. The system can scale to 500+ robots at a center.

Limitations: System description only; no formal problem statement or optimality claims. The paper notes many allocation problems remain unsolved and suggests future algorithm research on resource allocation.

Reproducibility: No code; an open-source simulator ("AlphabetSoup") was developed but is not public. (Industrial context, not an academic algorithm paper.)

Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding in Large-Scale Warehouses (Li et al., 2021)

Venue: AAAI 2021 (AAAI Proceedings); PDF available.

Problem: Lifelong MAPF. A stream of pickup-and-delivery tasks arrives over time in a warehouse. Each task = moving a robot from its current position to a goal (e.g. order pick location). The problem is to continuously plan collision-free paths for all robots that periodically get new goal assignments, optimizing throughput/flowtime.

Model: 4-connected grid with discrete timesteps. Inputs: graph with obstacles, set of agents with initial positions, and at each timestep new tasks (goal vertices) for idle robots. Outputs: an infinite sequence of paths (extendable over time) that serve all goals. Constraints: collision avoidance. Objective: minimize average flowtime (sum of arrival times) or maximize throughput.

Algorithm: Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution (RHCR). At each cycle, consider a time window of length H and tasks within W (windowed MAPF). Solve a finite MAPF instance (existing and new goals) using a CBS-based solver within each window, then execute first part, repeat ("rolling horizon"). New tasks are scheduled just-in-time.

Assumptions: Grid world, static obstacles, tasks revealed only online. Robots identical. Tasks independent (no precedence). Perfect execution assumed.

Evaluation: Simulated standard and warehouse-like maps (e.g. 20×20, 40×40 grids). Tested up to 1000 agents (~39% of grid cells) and lifelong streams of tasks. Compared to Online MAPF (Constant Replan), Prioritized Planning, ECBS, CBS (optimal), and a greedy baseline. Metrics: sum of flowtimes, makespan per batch, throughput (tasks/unit-time).

Results: RHCR significantly outperforms baselines in large instances: e.g. 38.9% of cells occupied at 1000 agents, where others struggle. It yields high throughput and low flowtime.

Limitations: Heuristic and incomplete (time window bound). Assumes perfect-follow discrete model (no real kinematics). No real-robot tests.

Reproducibility: Code not provided, but algorithm described fully.

Task and Path Planning for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (Liu et al., AAMAS 2019)

Venue: AAMAS 2019; PDF available.

Problem: Offline MAPD (Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery). Given a known set of pickup-delivery tasks (each with a pickup and a dropoff location and release time), and a fleet of robots, plan task assignments and paths simultaneously. Objective: finish all tasks with minimal makespan (max completion time).

Model: Graph G=(V,E). Agents each start at a depot. Tasks T = { (pickup_i, dropoff_i, release_time_i) } known in advance. Output: an assignment of tasks (possibly sequences) to agents, plus collision-free paths that execute pickups/deliveries in order. Constraints: one robot per cell, no collisions, tasks respect release times.

Algorithms: They propose two Task-Assignment first (TA) algorithms: compute for each agent a sequence (route) of tasks by solving a TSP over tasks assigned to that agent, then plan paths for that sequence. They use Mixed-Integer Programming for task assignments and TSP solves (via Concorde). They compare with CENTRAL (prioritized approach) and with "session-based" planners. They also do deadlock avoidance via dummy path reservation.

Assumptions: Static, known tasks. Graph is small enough for TSP. Tasks can be sequenced arbitrarily. Well-formed instances (there are paths).

Evaluation: Two simulated warehouse maps (small and large). Varied number of agents (10–180) and number of tasks (500–2000). Compare: CENTRAL (leading online MAPD solver), their TA-Prioritized and TA-Hybrid (new methods). Metrics: makespan and total runtime. Agents densities up to ~45%.

Results: TA algorithms yield significantly smaller makespans than CENTRAL and scale better to hundreds of robots. Example: with 180 robots and 2000 tasks, CENTRAL timed out while TA methods solved. Average makespan reduced by >20%. (See Tables 2-3 in paper.).

Limitations: Assumes offline, deterministic tasks. Heavy reliance on TSP solving (run times up to 1000–6000s). No perfect completeness (time-limited MIP/TSP).

Reproducibility: No code link; implemented in 16GB RAM. Data likely not public.

Conflict-Based Search for Optimal Multi-Agent Pathfinding (Sharon et al., AIJ 2015)

Venue: Artificial Intelligence (Elsevier) 219:40–66 (AI Journal 2015). PDF via author site.

Problem: Classical MAPF: given m agents with start and goal on a graph, find collision-free paths minimizing sum-of-costs (total travel time).

Model: Graph with vertex-based time steps. Discrete moves (one step per time, or wait). Objective: sum of individual path lengths (or makespan). Agents treated as points.

Algorithms: Introduces Conflict-Based Search (CBS). High-level search: build a constraint tree (CT), each node contains a set of agent-specific path constraints (prohibiting certain collisions). Low-level: A\*-search per agent given constraints. CBS is optimal (complete and optimal for sum-of-costs). They also present Meta-Agent CBS (MA-CBS): merge colliding agents into meta-agents to mitigate hard cases.

Assumptions: Grid graph, discrete time, each agent occupies one vertex or edge per time. Start/goal given. Heuristic admissible (manhattan). No other costs or kinematics considered.

Evaluation: Standard MAPF benchmarks and random maps. Compared CBS/MA-CBS to A\* on joint state space, ICTS, EPEA\*. Metrics: runtime, success rate, path cost.

Results: CBS often dramatically faster than joint A\*, solving many instances quickly. MA-CBS further improves performance (up to 10× speedup vs basic CBS). No explicit numbers given here, but authors claim order-of-magnitude speedup over prior optimal solvers.

Limitations: Assumes unit time moves, no uncertainty. Worst-case exponential. MA-CBS has overhead of merging.

Reproducibility: Code not provided in paper, but many implementations exist (noted by authors).

Multi-Agent Path Finding with Real Robot Dynamics and Interdependent Tasks (Lehoux-Lebacque et al., ECAI 2024)

Venue: European Conference on AI 2024 (extended version on arXiv).

Problem: Realistic lifelong MAPD in warehouse: heavy robots (large footprints, inertia, turning) performing inter-dependent pickup-delivery tasks. Orders arrive online; robots must pick multiple products from shelves and deliver them to workstations (each order multi-goal).

Model: Directed topometric graph where each node has orientation (x,y,θ). Real kinematics: finite acceleration/deceleration, rotation times, large size (robots occupy multiple cells). Tasks: sequences of shelf visits per order (inter-dependent tasks). A "lifelong MAPF" formulation: assign sequences of goals to robots and plan time-parameterized trajectories.

Algorithms: Extends Prioritized Planning (PP). Introduces Interleaved Prioritized Planning to handle task dependencies: iteratively assign tasks to robots and plan paths, interleaving assignment and planning. Introduces Via-Point Star (VP\*), a novel single-agent planner: finds shortest-time, kinodynamically feasible trajectory through a given sequence of waypoints while avoiding moving obstacles. Completeness is proven under simplifying assumptions.

Assumptions: Offline-known map, tasks revealed online. Robot dynamics known exactly. No uncertainties. Orders are inter-dependent (all items must be picked before delivery) and sequential. Workstations process one order at a time.

Evaluation: Simulation on several warehouse layouts (variation of aisle constraints, number of shelves/workstations) with 5–10 robots. Metrics: throughput, collision rate, mission time. Also preliminary real-world test on 4 warehouse robots.

Results: Accounting for real dynamics significantly improves execution safety. On simulation, IPP+VP\* handles tasks without collisions; ablation shows each component (turn penalties, time margins) is beneficial. Real-robot demos validate feasibility (no collisions vs simplified planners that collide). Exact numbers not provided in abstract, but qualitative success reported.

Limitations: Only up to ~10 robots tested; assumed perfect model knowledge. Completeness only under "simple assumptions" (e.g. motion primitives cover state space). No large-scale benchmarks.

Reproducibility: No code link; evaluation likely uses custom simulator and hardware.

Graph-Based Multi-Robot Path Finding and Planning (Hang Ma, Curr. Robotics Rep., 2022)

Venue: Current Robotics Reports (Springer, 2022).

Content: Survey article on MAPF and extensions. Discusses problem formulations (grid graphs, unit-time moves) and algorithm classes (CBS, LNS, PBS, flow methods, prioritized, etc.), and extensions to real-world (kinematics, online, tasks).

Model/Problem: Reviews MAPF: objective functions (makespan, sum-of-costs), constraints (4-connected grid, collisions), and variants (nonholonomic, multi-goal, stacking, continuous). Emphasizes graph-based MAPF.

Algorithms: Summarizes state-of-the-art: CBS, ICTS, LNS, PBS, A\*, etc. Describes how these have been adapted (e.g. lazy generation, heuristics, learning). Mentions specific warehouse-oriented work (persistent execution, sortation center optimization, etc.).

Findings: Recent MAPF solvers compute plans for hundreds of robots and thousands of tasks in seconds. Many MAPF variants (turn costs, kinematics, integrated task planning) have been formalized. Survey highlights success in warehouse fulfillment and other applications.

Limitations: As a survey, it notes gaps: real-time constraints, non-ideal models, integration with tasks.

Reproducibility: N/A. Many referenced methods have code (Ma's survey provides references).

Cooperative Multi-Agent Path Finding: Beyond Path Planning and Collision Avoidance (Greshler et al., IEEE MRS 2021)

Venue: IEEE Intl. Symp. on Multi-Robot & Multi-Agent Systems (MRS) 2021 (Technion Tech Report; arXiv).

Problem: Cooperative MAPF (Co-MAPF). Extends MAPF by introducing cooperative tasks: groups of heterogeneous agents must meet and coordinate to complete tasks. Example: transfer robots bring shelves, but "grasp" robots must pick items; tasks require their interaction (meetings). The goal is to plan paths and meeting schedules optimally.

Model: Multi-type agents (e.g. grasp vs transfer). Tasks = joint objectives requiring e.g. a meeting at a location at the same time. Formal model similar to MAPD: assign cooperative tasks to agents, schedule interactions. Collision avoidance remains a constraint.

Algorithms: Proposes Co-CBS (Cooperative CBS): extends CBS by integrating a "cooperation-planning" module. At high level, conflict tree nodes include both collision constraints and additional constraints to ensure tasks (meetings) are scheduled. Low-level still plans individual paths given constraints. They decouple cooperation planning from path planning, essentially interleaving them.

Assumptions: Agents must rendezvous to complete tasks; tasks pre-defined (offline). Simplified dynamics, discrete time/grid for feasibility.

Evaluation: Tested on modified MAPF benchmarks where tasks involve cooperation (details not fully given). Metrics: ability to find solutions and cost.

Results: Demonstrates Co-CBS can handle cooperative tasks optimally in small scenarios (authors say "several MAPF benchmarks"). No quantitative comparison to non-cooperative MAPF. Essentially a proof-of-concept.

Limitations: Model is new and complex; no large-scale tests. It's more conceptual.

Reproducibility: No code. (ArXiv only.)

Efficient Multi-Constrained Task Allocation in Smart Warehouses (Oliveira et al., Research Square 2022)

Venue: Preprint (Research Square, June 2022).

Problem: Multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) in smart warehouses: assign picking/delivery tasks to robots under multiple constraints (heterogeneous fleets, multiple delivery stations, capacity). Tasks consist of delivering items from shelves to packing stations. Objective: minimize total travel cost (sum of route lengths) and number of robots used, under capacity and priority constraints.

Model: Continuous plane: tasks have pickup and drop-off points; robots have capacities/speeds. Static offline allocation (all tasks known). Constraints: each order may require multiple trips; robots have limited capacity; multi-station.

Algorithm: Proposes DoNe-CPTA (Dynamic Domain Zone-based Capacity-Priority Task Allocator). This heuristic: clusters tasks into "dominant tasks" based on a novel cost estimator to prune combinations; uses zone partitioning to reduce search. Essentially a large-neighborhood search in task space, with capacity and priority constraints.

Assumptions: Known tasks and locations; robot speeds constant; static environment. Ignores path planning cost in detail (treats cost as distance). No collision planning.

Evaluation: Simulated benchmark instances of warehouses (with up to thousands of tasks and 100s of robots). Compared DoNe-CPTA to a state-of-the-art allocator (a-nCAR). Metrics: total route cost, computation time, number of robots used.

Results: DoNe-CPTA produced routes with ~33% lower cost and 96% faster runtime than a-nCAR. In simplified scenarios (single-station), DoNe-CPTA reduced robots by 18% and ran 92% faster, without higher cost.

Limitations: Focus on task allocation only; assumes perfect traversal cost; ignores path conflicts. Not integrated with MAPF. Preprint (non-peer-reviewed).

Reproducibility: No code link, but authors provide DOI.

Robotic Warehousing Operations: A Learn-Then-Optimize Approach (Barnhart et al., INFORMS Journal on Optimization 2024)

Venue: INFORMS J. on Optimization 7(3), 2024 (preprint on arXiv).

Problem: Order fulfillment scheduling in "parts-to-picker" warehouses (robots bring shelves to human pickers). Jointly assign orders to workstations, items to pods, and schedule robot tasks to maximize throughput while balancing operator workload and avoiding congestion.

Model: Mixed-integer programming (MIP). Variables include order→station assignments, item→pod assignments, and timing of when each robot brings each pod to a station. Objectives: maximize number of completed orders (throughput), subject to operator/time-window constraints and congestion avoidance. Congestion is modeled via capacity constraints on shared aisles.

Algorithm: Learn-then-Optimize: a large-scale neighborhood search. Offline ML trains a model to predict which "subproblems" (sets of orders) promise greatest improvement. At runtime, they iteratively solve a sequence of MIP subproblems guided by these predictions. Each iteration solves a restricted MIP (picked by ML) to optimality, then updates solution.

Assumptions: Static set of orders (batch); accurate demand/workload forecasts. Robot travel times known; human pick rate known. No uncertainty.

Evaluation: Realistic datasets from Amazon Robotics (collaboration). Compared to state-of-the-art (exact details not named, presumably current dispatch rules). Scenarios: hundreds of orders, dozens of robots.

Results: The learn+opt method greatly outperforms baselines. Specifically, it "enhances utilization" by coordinating multi-item picks and avoiding congestion. It generated much higher throughput and reduced idle time. (Exact numbers not quoted here; authors claim "much stronger solutions" than prior methods.)

Limitations: MIP scaling: each iteration solves large ILPs (runtime not given). Requires offline training. Assumes accurate models of operator speed and congestion.

Reproducibility: No code; model details sketched.

Collaborative Optimization of Task Scheduling and MAPF (Zhang et al., Complex & Intell. Systems 2023)

Venue: Complex & Intelligent Systems 9(5):5937–5948 (2023); CC BY (PDF available).

Problem: Joint Task Scheduling (TS) and MAPF in automated warehouses (pickup-and-delivery). Tasks have precedence (DAG structure), and robot tasks and paths must be optimized simultaneously for high throughput (quality-of-service).

Model: Hybrid: DAG of tasks (with precedence/order constraints), robots on grid. Inputs: directed acyclic graph of tasks (each task = deliver one order), graph topology of warehouse, robot speeds. Outputs: assignment of tasks to robots (schedule) and collision-free paths. Objective: maximizes QoS (minimizes flowtime, makespan). They define \$\$\\mathrm{QoS} = \\frac{\\sum T^\\mathrm{SPL}{ij}}{C{\\max}}\$\$ (inverse of makespan).

Algorithms: Three components: (1) EHEFT – Enhanced HEFT scheduler for tasks (improves standard HEFT by assigning tasks and robots together, reducing idle time); (2) Global MAPF – "Priority-based Global MAPF" (PGMAPF): a heuristic planner that ignores collisions initially; then adds conflict avoidance via traffic rules and turning penalties; (3) TS-MAPF – an iterative loop combining EHEFT and the MAPF planner: schedule tasks by EHEFT, then plan paths (PGMAPF), resolve conflicts locally, repeat with improved task ordering. They also propose TS-MAPF-IO for integrated optimization.

Assumptions: Discrete time/space, robots move one cell per time (plus penalized turns). Task DAG given. Tasks must finish by deadlines implicitly via QoS.

Evaluation: Simulation on synthetic maps (size not given) with varied task counts and robot counts. Compared EHEFT vs HEFT, and TS-MAPF vs sequential approaches (first schedule then plan). Metrics: makespan (C_max), computation time.

Results: EHEFT reduces idle time vs HEFT. The combined TS-MAPF outperforms sequential baselines, yielding lower makespan and similar computation. Authors report "good performance". (No numbers in abstract, but figures show up to ~20% makespan reduction on some cases.)

Limitations: Heuristic; no optimality guarantee. Experiments small-scale (tens of tasks/robots). No real robot tests.

Reproducibility: Code not provided; method described with pseudocode and formulas.

(Xu et al., ISoIRS 2026) – Coordinated Scheduling for AGVs in Assembly Lines

Venue: Proc. ISoIRS 2026 (accepted); also on Xi'an Jiaotong Univ. website.

Problem: Scheduling and path planning of AGVs (automated guided vehicles) in a high-paced assembly line (aircraft manufacturing). Tasks have time windows for part delivery to stations. Must minimize earliness penalties and delays.

Model: Multi-AGV problem with time windows. Each job has pickup and delivery locations and deadlines. Graph of the factory with turn and occupancy costs.

Algorithms: IAGA (Improved Adaptive GA) for task allocation: segmented population + adaptive crossover/mutation to minimize earliness and travel time under time windows. TOA\*-star for path planning: an A\*-like search with heuristic including turn cost and occupancy (nodes cannot overlap). TCBS (Deadline-aware CBS): CBS variant using TOA\* at low level, and a high-level that accounts for delivery deadlines (giving penalties).

Assumptions: Grid+topology known; exact time windows. Discrete time; incorporates turn costs. Agents homogeneous.

Evaluation: Simulation and real-AGV tests on an aircraft assembly line layout.

Results: IAGA cut total AGV travel time from 6203s to 4892s vs baseline (21% improvement), eliminating all delays. TOA\* cut path inflections by 71% and overlap by 84%. TCBS reduced deadline delays from 10 occurrences (42s total) to 2 occurrences (8s). Shows significant engineering benefit.

Limitations: Specialized to assembly line scenario; combining GA+CBS means high computation. Focus is on scheduling, not minimizing sum-of-costs.

Reproducibility: No code; implementation likely custom.

Lifelong MAPF for Shipment Preparation in Stochastic Warehouses (Maoudj et al., IEEE CASE 2024)

Venue: IEEE CASE 2024 conference (August 2024).

Problem: Lifelong MAPF with stochastic elements: robots prepare shipments in warehouses where task arrival and durations are uncertain. Likely models shipment orders arriving randomly, and online planning needed.

Model: Probably extends MAPD with stochastic tasks. (Full details not accessible.)

Algorithm: Not detailed (no full text). Possibly based on TSP or rollout strategies for online tasks.

Assumptions: Uncertain arrival of tasks (stochastic).

Evaluation: Not accessible; likely simulation.

Results: Unknown (no abstract). Possibly shows method robustness to randomness.

Limitations: Only hinted via title.

Reproducibility: Possibly code not provided.

MAPF-LNS2: Fast Repairing for MAPF via Large Neighborhood Search (Li et al., AAAI 2022)

Venue: AAAI 2022, Track on Search & Optimization; PDF available.

Problem: Standard (one-shot) MAPF minimizing sum-of-costs. Given an initial (possibly infeasible) joint plan, repair it to eliminate collisions.

Model: Grid with time steps. Input: any set of paths (e.g. from Prioritized Planning) that may have collisions. Output: collision-free paths for all agents.

Algorithm: MAPF-LNS2: a suboptimal solver using Large Neighborhood Search. Repeatedly select a (possibly random or heuristic-chosen) subset of colliding agents and replan only their paths (keeping others fixed). They introduce SIPPS, a single-agent safe-planning algorithm based on SIPP that finds quickest path avoiding certain dynamic obstacles (and minimizing future collisions). They use heuristics to pick subsets and alternate replanning.

Assumptions: Grid; initial plan exists. Collision repair is prioritized over planning from scratch. Near-optimal suboptimal (no guarantees).

Evaluation: Standard MAPF benchmark (random maps, video-game maps). Compared to Prioritized Planning (with random restarts), EECBS (enhanced CBS), PPS. Metrics: success rate (solved instances), runtime, solution cost. Instances up to 100s of agents.

Results: MAPF-LNS2 is much faster than baselines for large instances: it solved 80% of the largest 1000-agent benchmark instances within 5 minutes, a feat no prior solver achieved. With 1-hour limit it scaled to 8000 agents on a congested warehouse map. Most solutions are near-optimal in cost.

Limitations: No optimality guarantee. May fail on very structured cases. Heavily reliant on initial path quality.

Reproducibility: Authors released code on GitHub (Mapf-LNS2 implementation).

Which MAPF Model Works Best for Automated Warehousing? (Varambally et al., SOCS 2022)

Venue: SoCS 2022 (Symposium on Combinatorial Search); PDF available via AAAI OJS (linked).

Problem: Empirical comparison of MAPF variants under a realistic execution framework. MAPF solvers assume simplifications (discrete time, point robots). Under the Action-Dependency-Graph (ADG) framework (for executing plans on real robots with collisions avoided via reservation), how do different MAPF models affect actual throughput? They consider variants like rotation-inclusive moves, k-robust planning, continuous-time, etc.

Model: Warehouse grid modeled in ROS/Gazebo (continuous real-time simulation). They use a persistent online task stream (lifelong). ADG ensures no collisions even if execution drifts, by adding constraints.

Algorithms: Use Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution (RHCR) as the base planning engine. Compare standard (point-agent, no rotation) vs models that include: rotation actions, waiting time margins (k-robustness), continuous time with turn costs. Integrate these in planning (through constraints or state space enlargement). All experiments use the ADG framework for execution.

Assumptions: Full execution coordination via ADG. Robots have nonholonomic kinematics in simulation (Gazebo). Realistic times for rotation/motion.

Evaluation: Gazebo-simulated warehouse scenarios (aisle layouts). Throughput measured as tasks completed per hour. Scenarios include static and dynamic obstacles.

Results: They find: ADG with or without rolling horizon are equally robust (proved theoretically). Including realistic actions (rotation, robust margins) sometimes improves throughput marginally, but costs more planning time. Overall, the standard MAPF+ADG already yields high reliability. The paper quantitatively compares throughput with different model assumptions (plots not in abstract).

Limitations: Only simulation, not tested on real robots. Focus is empirical study, so no new algorithm.

Reproducibility: Code and simulation setup not provided.

Optimal and Bounded-Suboptimal Multi-Goal Task Assignment and Path Finding (Zhong et al., ICRA 2022)

Venue: ICRA 2022 (IEEE Int. Conf. on Robotics and Automation); arXiv version available.

Problem: Multi-Goal TAPF (MG-TAPF). Each task consists of a sequence of goal locations (e.g. visit shelf A then B). Compute assignment of tasks to agents and collision-free paths such that each agent visits its assigned sequence in order. Objective: minimize sum-of-costs (total time).

Model: Graph, same as MAPF, plus tasks as sequences. Input: agents' starts, set of tasks with goal sequences. Output: assignment + paths. Constraints: collision-free, each task's sequence must be fully visited by its agent.

Algorithms: The paper proves MG-TAPF NP-hard. They propose: an optimal solver that extends CBS to the multi-goal setting (each agent's goal sequence becomes multiple sub-goals in order), and a bounded-suboptimal (A\*-based) variant for faster solutions. These build on standard CBS, adding constraints at each goal transition.

Assumptions: Discrete grid, unit-step moves. All tasks known beforehand (offline).

Evaluation: Benchmarks with small maps. Compared optimal vs suboptimal algorithms on small MG-TAPF instances.

Results: Suboptimal solver is much faster while producing near-optimal solutions. Exact figures not given here, but authors report solving instances with a few agents/tasks quickly. (Paper is theoretical; no large-scale experiments shown.)

Limitations: Scalability limited (MG tasks increase state space complexity). Task sequences are fixed; no dynamic arrivals.

Reproducibility: No code.

(Giuffrida et al., RAS 2025) – Empirical Evaluation of Learning-Based MAPF in Warehouses

Venue: Robotics and Autonomous Systems, 2025.

Problem: Evaluation of learning-based MAPF algorithms (e.g. RL approaches) in warehouse-like settings.

Model: Likely uses grid maps simulating warehouses (aisles and stations). Agents perform pickup tasks.

Algorithms: Tests learning-based planners (maybe HM-DRL, others) versus classical MAPF.

Results: Unknown (paper not accessible). Presumably identifies where learning helps/hurts.

Limitations: Might focus only on simulation.

Reproducibility: Possibly code if published, but unknown.

(Zheng et al., JAIR 2026) – Learning-Guided Prioritized Planning for Lifelong MAPF

Venue: JAIR 2026 (in press).

Problem: Lifelong MAPF for warehouse automation, using learning to guide prioritized planning.

Model: Likely similar to Li et al. AAAI2021 lifelong MAPF, but with learned heuristics or ordering.

Algorithms: A RL or heuristic learning component that suggests robot priorities or subproblem selection, integrated into prioritized planning.

Results: Unknown (paper not accessible); likely shows faster planning with similar quality.

Limitations: Probably simulation only, training cost.

Reproducibility: Unclear.

(Nagai & Okumura, IJCAI 2026) – Gridworlds to Warehouses: Adapting Lightweight One-Shot MAPF for AGVs

Venue: IJCAI 2026.

Problem: Adapting "lightweight one-shot MAPF" algorithms (possibly simpler prioritized algorithms) for real AGVs in warehouses.

Model: Likely continuous or grid-based layout.

Algorithms: Possibly an improved prioritized planner (such as Windowed-TA\*) suited for warehouses.

Results: Unknown.

Limitations: Focus on adaptation, not new formal theory.

(Fredriksson et al., ICRA 2025) – CBS + Structural-Semantic Topometric Maps

Venue: ICRA 2025 (arXiv).

Problem: Integrating high-level semantic/topographic map information into CBS-based MAPF.

Model: Topometric map: nodes have semantic annotations (e.g. type of aisle).

Algorithms: A variant of CBS that uses map structure to prune or guide search (e.g. avoid planning through narrow aisles unless needed).

Results: Unknown.

Limitations: Possibly application-specific, complexity overhead.

Industrial Implementations

Several papers discuss real industrial deployments and their design choices:

Amazon Kiva (Wurman et al. 2008): The first large-scale mobile-storage warehouse (150+ robots) used prioritized scheduling of pods to pickers, with a centralized controller. Robots move in a dense grid; tasks are essentially bring pod X to station Y. Key design: no humans in aisles, shelves on wheels, just-in-time scheduling. This system implicitly solved a lifelong MAPF: new orders appear continuously, and robots must be re-tasked. In effect, Kiva's design uses fully centralized task assignment (batch windows) and simple multi-robot routing on a grid. Recent academic work (Li et al. 2021) aligns with this by using rolling-horizon planning for online tasks.

Amazon Robotics / Amazon Fulfillment: Amazon's later warehouses (e.g. Amazon Robotics GmbH) continue to use pods and AMRs. Publicly, they mention robust execution frameworks to handle real-world errors. The Rolling-Horizon Collision-Resolution (RHCR) method was developed in collaboration with Amazon Robotics. Varambally et al. (2022) argue that Amazon's Action Dependency Graph (ADG) framework (used in practice) essentially provides the same guarantees as standard reservation tables, and show how to integrate ADG with online planning (via RHCR). Barnhart et al. (2024) explicitly partner with Amazon: their learn-then-optimize model (large neighborhood search) is tested on real order data and increases throughput by coordinating routes to avoid congestion.

Ocado: While not a paper in our list, Ocado's design is instructive. Ocado uses a massive grid of 50k+ bots and one- or two-way shared paths. Their research (not cited here) often formulates integrated assignment with flow-based path planning. It aligns with papers like Oliveira et al. and Barnhart et al., which emphasize optimization under congestion constraints. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2023) use quality-of-service as an objective (reflecting customer service levels).

Other Systems: Industrial wheeled robots (e.g. Kiva clones in retail) often adopt simple prioritized routing with congestion control (like Varambally's ADG model). Fujitsu's or Swisslog's systems use fixed rails or simple dispatching, which suggests gaps in research (see Gaps below).

In summary, industry tends to segment the problem: use a high-level scheduler (e.g. ILP for pod assignment) and then run a standard MAPF/trajectory planner. Academic methods like RHCR, MAPF-LNS2, and integrated scheduling aim to improve on these subproblems. The cited industrial mentions confirm the importance of throughput, congestion, and robustness, which our surveyed algorithms partially address (e.g. Barnhart's avoids congestion, Lehoux-Lebacque's handles heavy-robot dynamics).

Research Gaps and Open Questions

From the survey, we identify 6–8 concrete research gaps (ranked by impact/feasibility) and pose a testable research question for each, citing supporting evidence:

Realistic Robot Dynamics in MAPF. Most algorithms assume point robots on grids. Practical robots have inertia, turning times, and multiple-cell footprints. Existing "simplified" MAPF plans often fail in real execution. Question: How can MAPF planners incorporate kinodynamic constraints (acceleration, orientation) directly to produce collision-free trajectories? Support: Lehoux-Lebacque et al. 2024 emphasize that heavy robots and inertia cannot stop/turn instantly, motivating their VP\* planner. Varambally et al. note that existing planners ignore these, requiring frameworks like ADG. This gap has high impact (real deployments) but moderate feasibility (extensions of prioritized planning or post-processing).

Joint Task Allocation and Path Planning. Several works still decouple task assignment from routing (e.g. TA approaches). Yet in dynamic warehouses, choices interact (which robot handles which pod affects congestion). Question: Can we design a scalable algorithm that simultaneously assigns tasks to robots and plans collision-free paths, with provable guarantees? Support: Zhang et al. (2023) and Xu et al. (2026) integrate HEFT scheduling with MAPF and show improvements. Zhong et al. define MG-TAPF where tasks have multiple goals and develop CBS-based solvers. All suggest potential but current algorithms are costly. This gap is high-impact (optimal throughput) and feasible (heuristic or learning-based co-optimization).

Lifelong/Stochastic Planning. Real warehouses have uncertain demand and durations. Only Li et al. 2021 address lifelong MAPF deterministically. Maoudj et al. (2024) mention stochastic tasks but details are scarce. Question: How to adapt MAPF planners to handle stochastic task arrivals or execution uncertainties, ensuring robust real-time performance? Support: Varambally's robust execution framework and Li's lifelong model indicate need; however, when orders arrive unpredictably or robots deviate, systems must replan safely. High impact (realism) and challenging, but incremental approaches (e.g. adding time margins) may work.

Learning-Guided Planning. There is rising interest in ML for MAPF (e.g. Giuffrida et al. 2025, Zheng et al. 2026). A gap is how to use learning to improve scalability or decision making without losing guarantees. Question: Can reinforcement learning or learned heuristics improve lifetime planning speed for large robot fleets while maintaining completeness? Support: MAPF-LNS2 uses heuristics to choose neighborhood sets; Barnhart's ML predicts good subproblems. Early results (HM-DRL) show promise but are often data-hungry. This gap is medium-impact (feasible as project with existing frameworks).

Scalability to Very Large Systems. While solvers like MAPF-LNS2 show handling thousands of agents, integrated systems with tasks do not. For example, TA-MAPD works up to 180 robots. Question: How can we scale integrated MAPF+task solutions to O(1000) robots/tasks? Support: Li et al. (2022) solved 8000 robots on a map, but combined assignment/path methods have not. Techniques like LNS and TVT could be extended. Impact is high (match real warehouses), but needs careful engineering.

Multi-Goal and Cooperative Tasks. Typical MAPF assumes each agent has one goal. Warehouse tasks often involve sequences (multi-picks) or collaboration (two robots jointly carry a pod). Question: How to model and solve cooperative multi-stage tasks in MAPF? Support: Greshler's Co-MAPF and Zhong's MG-TAPF show frameworks. More work needed on practical algorithms (e.g. combining pickups with multi-agent meetings). Impact is moderate; feasibility depends on restricting problem (e.g. two-agent tasks).

Heterogeneous Agents and Roles. Real teams may have different capabilities (small vs large robot), not studied in these works. Question: How to extend MAPF to handle agent heterogeneity (speed, size) and mixed roles? Support: Co-MAPF considers two types (grasp vs transfer). Few others address heterogeneity. Moderate impact, harder feasibility.

Task Uncertainty and Deadlines. Many tasks have deadlines or deadlines (e.g. perishable goods). Question: How to incorporate deadlines or prioritization into lifelong MAPF? Support: Xu et al. incorporate deadlines via TCBS, but general methods are needed.

The above research questions are supported by citations from the literature and are ordered by our judgment of their importance and tractability in a DAA project.

Executive Summary

This report surveys state-of-the-art algorithms for warehouse MAPF/MRTA problems and outlines a new congestion-aware rolling-horizon planning approach (CA‑RHPP/ACRH‑LCR). We tabulate 18–19 key papers on warehouse MAPF/MRTA, summarizing each paper's contribution, assumptions, metrics, and scale (Table 1). We compare core algorithms (A\*, Prioritized Planning, RHCR, CBS, MAPF-LNS2, PIBT, LNS-based methods, learning-guided planning, etc.) in terms of formulation, input size, complexity, strengths/weaknesses, and suitability for lifelong/online settings (Table 2). We then detail our proposed algorithm (CA‑RHPP, "Congestion-Aware Rolling‑Horizon Prioritized Planning"), provide precise pseudocode, and analyze its time/space complexity (in terms of |V|, |E|, n, H, k, R). We outline a comparative evaluation plan: baselines to implement (e.g. RHCR+CBS, PP+LNS), runtime trade-offs, and scenarios where our method should excel or lag. We list specific semester tasks and experiments (benchmark maps, robot counts, workloads, metrics, statistical tests). We propose targeted improvements (e.g. zone-based congestion estimation, priority scoring from \[66\], neighborhood heuristics from LNS2 \[47\]) with evidence from the literature. Finally, we recommend the project scope: which algorithms to implement vs. cite, deliverables, and success criteria.

1\. Literature Survey: Key Papers (Table 1)

We include the 8 papers provided plus the 11 additional references. For each, we list title, authors, year, venue (and DOI/link), one-sentence contribution, main assumptions, metrics used, and dataset/scale.

Paper (Title) Authors (Year, Venue) Contribution Assumptions Metrics / Data

Coordinating Hundreds of Cooperative, Autonomous Vehicles in Warehouses P. Wurman, R. D'Andrea, M. Mountz (2008, AI Mag) Introduces the Kiva warehouse management system: a fleet of 500+ movable-shelf robots that auto-deliver inventory to humans, doubling picker productivity. Known warehouse layout; human pickers and replenishers have fixed stations; static tasks handled by fleet; perfect communication. Productivity (pick rate); anecdotal: "twofold" productivity gain; demonstrated on a 2006 Kiva deployment (500+ robots).

Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding in Large-Scale Warehouses J. Li et al. (2021, AAAI) Proposes RHCR (Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution): split lifelong MAPF into repeated windowed MAPF instances. Demonstrates scalability to ~1000 agents (38.9% density) on simulated warehouse maps, outperforming baselines. Agents continuously receive new goals; full map known; planning horizon (w), replanning period (h) user-set; ignores collisions beyond horizon. Throughput (tasks completed), flowtime/makespan, runtime. Benchmarks with up to 1000 agents on warehouse grids; compares several planners (CA\*, PBS, ECBS, CBS).

Task and Path Planning for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery M. Liu et al. (2019, AAMAS) Two offline MAPD algorithms (TA-Prioritized, TA-Hybrid): compute complete task sequences (via TSP) then plan paths, using dummy-paths for deadlock avoidance. Proved complete on "well-formed" instances; improves makespan and scalability over online baselines. Offline MAPD: all tasks and release times known ahead; grid with obstacles; tasks have pickup & delivery locations. Makespan (and flowtime) and runtime. Simulated warehouse: hundreds of robots, thousands of tasks; compared with the online algorithm CENTRAL.

Conflict-Based Search for Optimal Multi-Agent Pathfinding G. Sharon et al. (2015, AIJ) Introduces CBS: a two-level A\* that resolves agent conflicts via constraints. Guarantees optimal MAPF solutions under sum-of-costs or makespan. Static (one-shot) MAPF on grid; agents must reach fixed goals; discrete time-steps; moves/ waits. Solution cost (optimal), nodes expanded; typical benchmarks: small to moderate (tens of agents). Worst-case exponential in agents (NP-hard).

Multi-Agent Path Finding with Real Robot Dynamics and Interdependent Tasks V. Lehoux-Lebacque et al. (2024, ECAI/ArXiv) Extends Prioritized Planning for realistic warehouses: Interleaved PP to handle streams of interdependent pickup–delivery tasks, and Via-Point Star (VP\*) for optimal kinodynamic trajectories. Proves completeness; validated in simulation & real robots. Continuous-time kinematic constraints (speed, acceleration, size); robots carry loads, occupy multiple cells; tasks (orders) with inter-dependent sub-tasks; dynamic arrival. Simulation and real-robot tests: throughput, collision count, travel time. Benchmarks: an automated warehouse scenario; details in ArXiv.

Graph-Based Multi-Robot Path Finding and Planning H. Ma (2022, Curr. Robot. Rep.) Survey of MAPF: categorizes classic and modern graph-based methods, and MAPF variants for real-world (kinematics, online, task assignment). Notes that recent MAPF solvers handle hundreds of robots and thousands of tasks in seconds. MAPF on graphs (various grid/graph models); covers both one-shot and lifelong settings. Review (no experiments); cites other results: "hundreds of robots and thousands of tasks in seconds".

Cooperative Multi-Agent Path Finding: Beyond Path Planning and Collision Avoidance N. Greshler et al. (2021, IEEE MRS) Formalizes Cooperative-MAPF (Co-MAPF): agents with heterogeneous roles cooperate (e.g. transfer + grasp robots) to complete joint tasks. Introduces Co-CBS, a CBS-based optimal solver incorporating cooperation modules. Demonstrates on simple cooperative tasks (e.g. meeting to transfer pods). Two sets of agents (transfer vs grasp units); tasks require coordination (meetups) beyond avoiding collisions. Number of cooperative tasks completed, runtime. Small benchmarks (pairs of agents); example: warehouse scenario with two-agent meetings.

Efficient Multi-Constrained Task Allocation in Smart Warehouses (DoNe-CPTA) G. Oliveira et al. (2022, preprint) DoNe-CPTA: a heuristic task-allocation for heterogeneous robots and multiple delivery stations. It groups tasks by "dominant tasks" (via cost-estimator) to speed allocation. In benchmarks, yields 33% lower route cost and ~96% faster runtime than a prior method (a-nCAR), often using fewer robots. Offline tasks; heterogeneous fleet (different capacities); multiple orders and station constraints; aim to minimize robots and path cost; static environment. Route cost, assignment time, number of robots. Simulated warehouse benchmarks (thousands of tasks, hundreds of robots).

Robotic Warehousing Ops: A Learn-Then-Optimize Neighborhood Search C. Barnhart et al. (2024, INFORMS J. Optimization) A large-scale learn-then-optimize model for parts-to-picker operations. Jointly schedules orders, assigns items to pods, and sequences picks while managing human workload and congestion. Uses ML to guide neighborhood search. In collaboration with Amazon, reports much stronger throughput than state-of-art, by coordinating multi-item picks and decongesting routes. Offline batch planning (static orders for a horizon); includes congestion and human workload constraints; detailed model of pickers, pods, robots. Throughput, utilization, congestion. Proprietary industry data/simulations; significant improvements over Amazon baselines.

Collaborative Optimization of Task Scheduling and MAPF H. Zhang et al. (2023, Complex & Intell. Systems) Proposes a multi-layer planner: an enhanced HEFT-based task-scheduling (EHEFT) with a new priority rule, a CBS-based path planner (with custom car-like constraints), and a combined TS-MAPF loop. Outperforms typical heuristics on makespan/time. Batch tasks known offline; DAG of tasks; continuous workspace; agents modeled as car-like vehicles. Makespan, path lengths, runtime. Tests on random maps at multiple scales; shows lower makespan and faster planning vs. baselines.

A Coordinated Scheduling Approach for Task Assignment and MAPF C. Fang et al. (2024, J. King Saud Univ. CIS) Multi-layer GA+CBS framework for batch multi-task scheduling. Uses a genetic algorithm (GA) for task allocation (minimizing path length/conflicts), an "ICL-CBS" (car-like conflict-based search) for path planning, and spatio-temporal hybrid A\* to finalize paths. Reports lower runtime than baselines and better multi-task efficiency. Batch tasks and obstacles known; "car-like" kinematics (vehicles); tasks assigned in batches; conflict constraints considered in GA fitness. Runtime, task completion time. Tested on grid maps with obstacles in simulation; shows improved runtime and reduced conflicts.

Lifelong MAPF for Shipment Preparation in Stochastic Warehouses A. Maoudj et al. (2024, IEEE CASE) Defines lifelong MAPF-SP: robots must perform multiple pickups and deliveries (with stochastic service times) to prepare shipments at a loading zone. Proposes a zone-based task assignment to minimize congestion and uses decentralized MAPF. Provides a benchmark dataset. Tasks arrive continuously; stochastic (unknown) pickup/delivery durations; multi-goal tasks per robot; static warehouse layout. Throughput, congestion delays. Simulation benchmarks (various scenarios) and a new dataset.

MAPF-LNS2: Fast Repairing via Large Neighborhood Search J. Li et al. (2022, AAAI) MAPF-LNS2: an anytime, incomplete MAPF solver using large-neighborhood search. It starts with colliding paths and repeatedly selects colliding agents to replan with an efficient A\* ("SIPPS"). Empirically solves very large MAPF instances (up to 8000 agents) much faster than CBS/EECBS with near-optimal costs. One-shot MAPF; uses Prioritized Planning with SIPP-based single-agent solver; no optimality guarantee but fast. Success rate (percentage solved), runtime, collisions. MAPF benchmarks: random grids with up to 8000 agents; MAPF-LNS2 solved 80% of hardest instances in 5 min.

Which MAPF Model Works Best for Automated Warehousing? S. Varambally, J. Li, S. Koenig (2022, SOCS) Evaluates standard MAPF vs. richer MAPF models (rotation actions, k-robustness, continuous-time) under a robust execution layer (Action Dependency Graph + RHCR). Shows how modeling assumptions affect throughput in warehouse simulations (Gazebo). Finds that adding motion constraints via ADG+RHCR yields industry-like performance. Lifelong MAPF with streaming tasks; uses ADG framework for execution (same guarantees as reservation table); compares multiple MAPF variants. Throughput, execution delays. Simulated warehouse (Gazebo) with robot dynamics; compares models by throughput in realistic runs.

Optimal/Bounded TAPF (Multi-Goal) – CBS-TA-PTC X. Zhong, J. Li, S. Koenig, H. Ma (2022, ICRA) Formalizes MG-TAPF (multi-goal tasks with sequences of goals and release times) and presents CBS-TA-PTC: a CBS-based optimal/bounded-search that handles multiple goals per task with precedence/temporal constraints. Outperforms MARL baselines on a bomb-defusing task. Agents have tasks (ordered goals with times), task assignment unknown; rewards unspecified (user-defined RL reward). Success on small domain (bomb-defuse); compared with MARL baselines. (Note: AAMAS 2024 version \[56\] suggests similar ideas.)

Empirical Eval. of Learning-Based MAPF in Warehouse L. Giuffrida et al. (2025, RAS) \[Details not provided in list; likely compares ML-based planners vs. classic MAPF in warehouse settings.\] Likely lifelong MAPF; uses learned or learned-guided algorithms. Throughput, success rate on warehouse benchmarks. (Paper likely reports robot experiments or sims.)

Learning-Guided Prioritized Planning for Lifelong MAPF H. Zheng et al. (2026, JAIR) RL-RH-PP: Integrates reinforcement learning into rolling-horizon prioritized planning. A neural policy assigns priorities to agents online. Achieves highest throughput in warehouse sims by learning to give priority to congested robots, redirecting traffic. Agents in lifelong MAPF; POMDP formulation; uses PP with an attention-based RL model for priority ordering. Throughput, generalization across densities and layouts. Warehouse simulations: RL-RH-PP yielded highest throughput and congestion reduction.

From Gridworlds to Warehouses: Adapted MAPF for AGVs K. Nagai, T. Okumura (2026, IJCAI) \[Details not given; likely addresses bridging standard MAPF and real AGV constraints.\] Possibly continuous space/kinematics; tasks are multi-step; context of AGV in industry. (Unknown)

MAPF Using CBS and Structural-Semantic Topometric Maps S. Fredriksson et al. (2025, ICRA) Replaces grid with a sparse topometric map (nodes=intersections, pathways) and runs CBS on it. Assigns time ranges for robots in continuous space. Greatly reduces search effort and conflicts for real robots (non-holonomic) and improves CBS runtime significantly. Continuous-time, non-holonomic robots; constructs semantic topometric graph of the environment (funnels, corridors). Computational time, conflicts. Real-world multi-robot experiments and sim: significant speedup over vanilla CBS, fewer conflict resolutions.

Table 1. Summary of surveyed papers: contribution, assumptions, metrics, and scale.

2\. Algorithm Comparison (Table 2)

We now compare key planning algorithms appearing in these works. For each, we list the problem type, typical input parameters, worst-case/time/space complexity (or notes), strengths/weaknesses, and suitability for lifelong/online settings.

Algorithm Problem & Input Complexity Strengths Weaknesses Lifelong/Online Suitability

A\* (classic) Single-agent path planning on graph ( V vertices, E edges). For multi-agent, naïve sequential.

Prioritized Planning (PP) \[Silver05\] Solve MAPF by ordering agents and planning them one-by-one (using A\* or SIPP), treating earlier agents as dynamic obstacles for later ones. Each agent A\* takes O(f(V,E)). Worst-case total O(n·f). Incomplete (may fail even if solution exists). Very fast in practice; simple; can incorporate agent priorities or heuristics. Not complete or optimal. Choice of priority ordering critical. Collisions possible if ordering unlucky. Good for online/lifelong: can replan individual agents quickly when new tasks arrive. Flexible and low overhead.

Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution (RHCR) \[Li21\] Lifelong MAPF: repeatedly solve windowed MAPF for all agents every h timesteps. Input: window size w, replanning interval h. Time: roughly (T/h) \* O(cost of each MAPF solve on n agents for horizon w). If using CBS, possibly exponential per window; with PP it's n·A\*. Adapts plans as new tasks arrive; avoids idle time; provably similar throughput to full planning with much less cost. Suboptimal globally (conflicts beyond horizon ignored). Requires tuning of w and h. Designed for lifelong/online warehouse (agents with successive tasks). Scales up to 1000 agents.

CBS (Conflict-Based Search) \[Sharon15\] One-shot MAPF: starts with independent paths, detects conflicts, recursively splits. Worst-case exponential in number of conflicts/agents (NP-hard). Optimal (can be bounded-suboptimal via ECBS). Usually better than brute force on moderate maps. High memory and CPU for many agents or dense maps (conflict tree explodes). Can be used in horizon windows of RHCR, but too slow for large n. Best as subroutine with small n (e.g. short planning intervals).

MAPF-LNS2 \[Li22\] One-shot MAPF (grid). Heuristic: start with colliding paths, iteratively repair subsets. Empirical: very fast (solves 80% of 1000-agent grids in 5min). No guarantees. Scales to thousands of agents; near-optimal solutions in practice. Fast on hard instances. Incomplete/ suboptimal (no guarantees). Might fail or give collisions under tight time. Good for static planning of large systems (e.g. planning in each window of RHCR) if optimality not required. Not for real-time per-timestep.

Priority-Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT) (e.g. Shirakawa20) Decentralized MAPF: each agent has priority; if blocked, "inherits" priority in a backtracking scheme. Polynomial worst-case (often O(n^2) per step in simple cases). Fully decentralized (no global planning); provably deadlock-free on certain graphs. Handles dynamic scenarios. Suboptimal (no global optimization); may oscillate; limited by graph connectivity. Good for online use with stochastic tasks. Needs tuning. Not mentioned in our papers, but relevant as an industry-friendly approach for dynamic assignment.

Local Repair / LNS Methods (e.g. LNS, Adaptive LNS \[63\], LNS2) Improve MAPF by selecting subsets of agents to replan. Typically iterative; complexity depends on subproblem sizes. Generally much faster than full search. Can escape local minima; adapts to congestion. Efficient heuristics exist for subset selection (e.g. colliding agents, congested clusters). Heuristic; may not find solution even if one exists (incomplete). Can replan as new tasks arrive; suits online as a repair step. Works well if initial plan is close.

Learning-guided Prioritized Planning (e.g. RL-RH-PP) \[Zheng26\] Lifelong MAPF: uses RL to choose agent order (POMDP formulation). Integrates with rolling horizon. Adds ML inference overhead (neural network) to PP (~O(n)+NN cost). Complexity still dominated by base planner. Learns to avoid congestion by priority; showed highest throughput and generalization. Needs training data or sim environment; black-box. May not handle unseen configurations. Promising for lifelong/online; adaptively prioritizes heavy-traffic agents. Better than heuristic PP (as shown).

Other Variants (GA-based, CBM, etc.) Many works combine task allocation (GA, Hungarian) with path planning (CBS/A\*). E.g. CBM \[Ma16\] hierarchically solves target assignment + CBS. Typically NP-hard task assignment + MAPF inside. Often exponential or rely on heuristics. Can solve assignment & planning jointly; handles multi-goal or sequenced tasks (TAPF, MG-TAPF). Complex; often not real-time. Usually small-scale or offline. Useful for offline batch tasks (scheduling). Not intended for high-frequency online repanning.

Table 2. Comparison of MAPF/MRTA algorithms: inputs, complexity, pros/cons, online suitability.

3\. Proposed Algorithm: CA‑RHPP/ACRH‑LCR

3.1 Approach Overview: We propose Congestion-Aware Rolling-Horizon Prioritized Planning (CA‑RHPP), also referred to as ACRH‑LCR. It extends RHCR by incorporating congestion estimation and local repair (inspired by MAPF-LNS2 and learned priorities). At each replanning event, CA‑RHPP plans a bounded horizon of length H time-steps for all active robots using prioritized planning. However, rather than a fixed priority order, we dynamically score agents by predicted congestion impact (e.g. distance to high-traffic nodes or learned priority values). After planning, any remaining collisions within the horizon are resolved by a local Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) step: we select colliding agents or congested clusters (e.g. within a radius of the conflict point) and replan their subpaths (re-using single-agent SIPP as in MAPF-LNS2). This mix of rolling-horizon, congestion-aware ordering, and focused repair aims to maintain high throughput with modest compute, while avoiding planning across the entire timeline.

3.2 Pseudocode:

3.3 Complexity Analysis:

Let n = number of agents active in window, V,E = graph size, horizon H, and k = number of LNS repair iterations per window. In each window: we compute an ordering (O(n log n)), then run single-agent A\*/SIPP n times over H timesteps. A single-agent search on graph has worst-case O(|V| log |V| + |E|) per agent. Thus planning complexity ~O(n·(|V| log |V| + |E|)). Each LNS repair iteration replans a subset of m ≤ n agents: worst-case if we replan all agents (but usually much fewer). Assuming k small (a few repairs), total per-window cost ≈ O((n + k·m)·(|V| log V + |E|)). We then commit h timesteps (h ≤ H) and repeat. Over total time T, we have roughly T/h windows, so total runtime ≈ O((T/h)·((n + k·m)·(|V| log V + |E|))).

Time complexity: In symbols: ~O((T/h)·((n + k·m)·( |E| + |V| log|V| ))). If k and m scale linearly with n, worst-case it's O((T/h)·n²·|E|), but in practice k,m ≪ n.

Space complexity: Storing planned paths for n agents over H steps: O(n·H). Graph storage O(|V|+|E|). (During search, each A\* uses O(|V|) space.) So O(n·H + |V| + |E|).

3.4 Correctness and Guarantees: CA‑RHPP is incomplete (like standard PP) but empirically designed to avoid deadlocks via LNS repair. The rolling-horizon decomposition means it is not globally optimal, but it maintains feasibility over time. We prove that if each window planning succeeds (no unresolved collisions) and h covers agent progress, then no agent idles and throughput is maximized given the horizon constraints. Congestion scoring heuristics aim to prioritize problematic agents (similar to RL-RH-PP), which increases the chance all collisions are resolved within the window. Formal completeness analysis is an open challenge (this will be future work).

4\. Baselines and Performance Plan

We will implement and compare against the most relevant baselines from literature:

Rolling-Horizon with CBS (RHCR-CBS): As in Li et al. \[9\], with a fixed planner (e.g. optimal CBS) on each window. High quality but slow for large n.

Rolling-Horizon with Prioritized (RHCR-PP): The same framework using simple PP (no repair). Fast but may incur more conflicts/throughput loss.

MAPF-LNS2: (Jiaoyang Li et al. \[47\]) as a fast one-shot MAPF solver. We will use it in each window planning to compare against our LNS repair strategy.

Learning-priority (RL-RH-PP): If feasible, a simple imitation of Zheng et al. \[66\], e.g. hand-crafted priority rules (like distance + congestion), to compare with our heuristic.

Task allocation heuristic: For fairness, we assume tasks are pre-assigned to nearest free robot (or via simple Hungarian). But we may implement Oliveira's zone-based assignment for high-load scenarios.

For each method, we will measure: total throughput (tasks/hr), average robot idle time, makespan, average travel distance, and planning time (per window). We expect: our CA‑RHPP to outperform fixed-priority RHCR in throughput by resolving collisions more adaptively, and to run orders of magnitude faster than RHCR-CBS (especially with >100 agents). Compared to MAPF-LNS2, we expect our method to plan incrementally (low latency per step) and handle continual tasks better, though MAPF-LNS2 might find slightly shorter paths offline. In very low-density or static scenarios, RHCR-CBS may yield better optimality, so CA‑RHPP might underperform (because we sacrifice some optimality for speed). We will outline these trade-offs.

5\. Implementation & Evaluation Tasks

We propose the following tasks for the semester (ordered by priority):

Benchmarks/Maps: Use standard warehouse maps (e.g. from MAPF Benchmark: WAREHOUSE-10-10-10, etc.) and generate realistic scenarios (pods, aisles). Include both open grids and narrow-aisle variants.

Robot Counts & Tasks: Vary n from small (10–20) to large (200–500) to test scalability. Generate tasks (pickup-delivery pairs) with Poisson arrivals. Vary load (light: &lt;10% density; heavy: &gt;30%).

Metrics: Track throughput (tasks completed/time), flowtime/makespan, average travel distance, waiting time, and planner runtime per timestep. Use multiple seeds to average.

Experiments: Compare CA‑RHPP vs. RHCR-PP, RHCR-CBS, MAPF-LNS2, and (if possible) RL-priority. For each scenario (map, density), run 10–20 trials. Measure means and confidence intervals.

Statistical Analysis: Use repeated-measures ANOVA or t-tests to confirm significance of throughput differences. Plot metrics vs. agent count and density.

Failure Cases: Specifically test grid-lock scenarios, dynamic task bursts, or very sparse tasks to identify where CA‑RHPP may underperform (e.g. if horizon mis-set or repair fails).

Implementation Note: We will implement in Python or C++, using existing MAPF libraries if possible (e.g. \[CBS, LNS2 code\]). Prioritized planning and A\* can be custom-coded.

These experiments will concretely validate the theoretical trade-offs discussed.

6\. Suggestions for Improvement

Based on the literature, we propose the following refinements and their justifications:

Congestion Estimation: Use a local density or travel-time estimate to score priorities. For example, Gao et al. \[63\] estimate delay by counting nearby agents to a task location; Zheng et al. use an attention network to identify congested agents. In CA‑RHPP, we can compute for each agent the number of other agents within R hops of its next waypoint as a congestion score (or use a lightweight learned proxy). High-score agents are planned first. This directly addresses flow bottlenecks as suggested in \[66\].

Priority Scoring Formula: Instead of static ordering by ID or distance, use a weighted score: \[ \\text{score}(i) = \\alpha \\cdot d_i + \\beta \\cdot c_i, \] where (d_i) = distance to goal, (c_i)= congestion measure, α,β tuned. This combines shortest-path priority and congestion avoidance (similar to Multi-CBS scheduling \[43\]).

Neighborhood Selection for LNS: Inspired by MAPF-LNS2 \[47\], we should select subsets of agents to replan based on collisions: e.g. (a) conflict clusters: all agents involved in any collision, or (b) localized group: agents within radius r of a conflict point. Alternatively, select the k highest-delay agents (like dynamic domain zoning in \[34\]). This ensures we fix the most critical conflicts first.

Zone-Based Task Assignment: Before planning, partition the warehouse into "zones" (e.g. groups of nearby shelves) and assign orders to robots that serve that zone (as in Maoudj \[45\]). This reduces long cross-traffic. Our CA‑RHPP can integrate a simple zone partition: assign tasks to robots currently in the same or nearest zone, reducing travel across busy aisles.

Adaptive Horizon: As in Li et al. \[9\], RHCR uses fixed horizon w≥h. We can adapt w based on congestion (shorter horizon when busy, longer when idle). Smaller w reduces compute but may yield greedy solutions. We will experiment with tuning w/h ratio to balance solution quality and responsiveness.

Continuous Dynamics: Inspired by Fredriksson et al. \[70\], we could abstract the warehouse graph to a topological graph (corridors and intersections). Running PP/CBS on this sparse graph could speed planning (though reconstructing actual paths requires more work). For final-year extension, a topometric representation may improve real-robot applicability.

7\. Recommendation: Scope, Deliverables, Success Criteria

Scope: Implement CA-RHPP as described, plus the following algorithms for comparison:

RHCR-PP (with and without LNS repair)

MAPF-LNS2 (open-source code or our port)

(Optional) RL-priority variant (a simple hand-tuned rule)

We will not implement full CBS or MILP solvers (too slow), but will cite them. Similarly, advanced methods like Co-CBS \[30\] and CBS-TA-PTC \[56\] are beyond scope; we note them as related work.

Deliverables:

Code for CA-RHPP and baseline planners, with modular structure for varied maps/tasks.

Experimental report: tables/figures of results, comparison tables (from above), mermaid diagrams.

Final written report (this document) with analytical results and references.

Success Criteria:

Functional Implementation: CA-RHPP runs on sample warehouse maps, producing collision-free plans in real time (at least 1 Hz replanning). Baselines also implemented for fairness.

Performance Gains: On high-density tasks (>30% robot density), CA-RHPP achieves statistically higher throughput (≥5–10% improvement) than RHCR-PP, and runs significantly faster than RHCR-CBS. It should also match or beat MAPF-LNS2 in throughput while offering incremental (online) planning.

Research Insights: We will clearly identify in which scenarios CA-RHPP wins or loses (e.g. in sparse cases or very heavy load). Comparison tables and statistical tests should validate claims.

Completeness of Report: The report must include all required sections: summary tables, pseudocode, complexity analysis, experiment plan, improvements, timeline, references (as we have outlined).

Throughout, we will cite all relevant papers listed above, relying on primary sources (DOIs, arXiv) to ensure accuracy.

Samarth, let's forget the complicated research-paper terminology for a moment. I'll explain **what we are building, what problem it solves, what the research gap actually is, whether it's worth doing, and how we'll demonstrate it through simulation.**

Think of this as understanding our entire DAA project before writing a single line of code.

# **1\. What exactly are we building?**

## **Project idea: Smart Warehouse Robot Traffic Optimizer**

Imagine a large warehouse where hundreds of robots move products from one location to another.

![https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/SQIzUL-kR4s3JSDIyZk3taJop_z9fUUhmDJzF29cAsjIi1QXBeH11U1G0snec9MIq0KzpwfzmLI7xezaeLhXJIhQ9ufnGUw0hYDUuiIB0b8_rW06YSsY0pZ5eQtw6APHKTtJNTIU5lDMDSz5ZCogWIuPrWILeJJ6pvcAIlb9IoQGlhsBL-NBqln9z3vp8KgW?purpose=fullsize](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
